detailed_rack: No roped rock rack is carried on this route. The non-standard North Ridge (via the Wolf Creek/Gardner Meadows trail and an old, largely-vanished mine boot path) is an unroped Class 2-3 scramble: talus and scree to Gardner Meadows, then an unmaintained path/cairns to a tarn and a spur ridge onto the crest, then a choose-your-own-line scramble along the ridge crest with a few class 3 moves on a spur ridge. Parties do not place cams or nuts or use a rope.
pro_needs: None placed — this is unprotected scrambling, not protected rock climbing. Hazard is loose rock/footing (talus, scree, old mining debris) rather than lack of gear placements; a helmet is the relevant safety item, not a rack.
what_to_bring: helmet (loose rock/rockfall risk on talus and scree)
trekking poles for scree and talus
ice axe and/or microspikes if snow lingers near the tarn or on the spur ridge (common into early summer on this east-side, north-facing approach)
sturdy boots with good ankle support for off-trail talus
map/compass or GPS — the old mine boot path is faint to nonexistent above Gardner Meadows, marked only by occasional cairns and cut logs
extra water — long ridge approach (about 10 miles of trail to Gardner Meadows) with few reliable water sources higher up

detailed_rack: No rope or rack needed for the standard scramble; solid footwear and, for many, trekking poles for the talus are sufficient.
pro_needs: None — this is an unroped class 2-3 scramble; a light rope/rack is only useful for a party wanting extra security through the gendarme band.
what_to_bring: ice axe and traction (possible early-season snow on the lake and upper slopes)
extra water (Scatter Lake is the last reliable source)
sun protection for the exposed upper ridge

detailed_rack: Doubles of cams from 0.4 in to #3 with a few smaller cams and one #4-equivalent; full nut set. Helmet recommended for loose rock and lichen-covered holds.
pro_needs: Standard double rack in the small-to-mid range covers the crack/flake climbing; the minimal-gear P7 bulges reward careful, patient placements.
what_to_bring: Approach shoes for the talus/scree approach
water treatment for the Early Winters Creek crossing
bivy gear if splitting the approach over two days

detailed_rack: A light rock rack (small-to-medium cams/nuts) for the low-5th-class ridge pitches and the 5.8 chimney, plus a rope, rappel device, and gear for a snow couloir descent (axe, and ideally pickets/flukes for the descent).
pro_needs: Standard alpine trad rack sufficient for sustained 4th/low-5th class with a short 5.8 crux; snow protection (flukes/pickets) needed for the descent couloir rather than the ascent itself.
what_to_bring: Multi-day backpacking/camping gear for a 4-5 day trip
Approach shoes plus climbing shoes/boots suited to 5.8
Headlamp (long summit days reported into the night)

detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard West Route. From Upper Cathedral Lake it follows a boot path around the west ridge, then scree/grass slopes to a basin (~8,000 ft), then easy slopes south to the summit. The true (south) summit has one short mantle move onto a block; otherwise it's a walk.
pro_needs: No trad gear is placed on the standard route - it is a scree/talus/grass walk-up with one short 3rd-class move near the true summit. A rope/harness/rack is only relevant if linking into one of the technical buttress routes (Middle Finger Buttress, Finger of Fatwa, Pilgrimage to Mecca) on the same peak.
what_to_bring: ice axe and possibly crampons for lingering snow before ~mid-July
sun protection - long exposed alpine walk
map/GPS - open terrain with braided boot paths

detailed_rack: Pickets if uncomfortable with sustained 35-50 degree snow, a set of stoppers, cams, and webbing for rappel anchors; single or double ice axes and crampons for the couloir.
pro_needs: Ample rock protection is available on the walls flanking the couloir if it turns icy; the exit pitch and summit-ridge scrambling take standard rock gear.
what_to_bring: Helmet - rockfall/icefall risk in the couloir
Glacier travel gear for the Colchuck Glacier descent
Extra layers - the couloir is often shaded and cold

detailed_rack: No roped rock rack is used on this route. Arrowhead's South/standard route is a non-technical Class 2-3 scramble — travel is on logging road, open clearcut, ridge, and a short rocky summit step, with no crack systems or fixed anchors that parties place gear in. Every trip report reviewed describes it as unroped; no cams, nuts, or rope appear in any gear list. The route is most commonly climbed Dec-April as a winter/spring snow scramble, in which case an ice axe and crampons (or microspikes, swapped depending on snow firmness) substitute for a rock rack as the real protection system, used for self-arrest and traction on the steep upper ridge (~5,100ft+) and near tree wells/cornices. A summer ascent (July-Aug) trades snow travel for brush/talus and the same short Class 3 rock step, typically done in approach shoes with hands only.
pro_needs: No fixed or removable rock protection is placed — this is an unroped scramble, not a roped climb. In winter/spring conditions, self-arrest with an ice axe is the primary safety system on the steep upper ridge, and crampons provide the real 'protection' on hard, icy, wind-swept snow. The Class 3 summit rock step is short and low-angle; parties comfortable with exposed unroped scrambling solo it without gear. Rock quality on the short summit block is unknown — treat with normal alpine caution for an unfrequented Cascades summit block.
what_to_bring: map, compass, and altimeter or GPS — clearcuts, logging roads, and open ridge terrain are easy to lose in poor visibility
headlamp — several trip reports logged 6-7.5+ hour car-to-car days

avalanche safety gear (beacon, probe, shovel) for winter/spring ascents — accounts disagree on how avalanche-exposed the standard route is (one TR calls it 'avalanche-safe', others describe 'considerable avalanche terrain' on nearby lines), so carry standard winter travel gear and judgment
wind layers for the exposed upper ridge

detailed_rack: Medium sport rack: 10-12 quickdraws for bolts, set of wired stoppers (sizes 1-4) for slab cracks, medium nuts (sizes 1-3), 60m dynamic rope, belay device, 4-6 locking carabiners.
pro_needs: Lead climber comfortable on 5.9 with mix of bolt and natural gear protection. Good slab footwork and crack climbing fundamentals essential.

detailed_rack: Light sport rack with 12+ quickdraws for bolted protection. Bring wired stoppers and medium-sized nuts for occasional slab placements. Single 60m dynamic rope, belay device, 4-6 locking carabiners.
pro_needs: Lead climber comfortable on 5.10b slab with bolted protection. Basic trad skills for occasional nut placements helpful but not essential.
rack: Wired stoppers and nuts (optional, for occasional slab placements)

detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed — this is a Class 2-3 snow/glacier mountaineering route, not a roped rock climb. No party is known to use cams, nuts, or pitons. Parties describe dirt/scree gullies with loose rock on the lower south approach and open, generally low-angle glacier/snow slopes above — none describe placing rock protection. Carry a thin glacier-travel rope (roughly 30m per 2-3 person rope team) and a basic crevasse-rescue kit (harness, 2-3 prusik cords or a Tibloc/Micro Traxion, small pulley, a few locking biners and slings) for the Diobsud Creek Glacier and Green Lake Glacier crossings.
pro_needs: No fixed rock protection is needed or used on this route — it is snow/glacier travel with a brushy/loose-rock approach gully, not technical rock climbing. Crevasse hazard on the Diobsud Creek and Green Lake Glaciers is real but variable by season: parties describe crossing unroped when the glacier is well filled-in with no visible cracks (one party found no visible crevasses but probed for them as a precaution, and a party on a nearby route mentions crossing a moat), while a party on a slightly later-season visit found crevasses beginning to open up and hidden snow bridges, prompting the party to parallel crevasse lines carefully. A thin glacier rope and basic crevasse-rescue kit (prusiks or a Tibloc-style device) is the prudent standard setup rather than a rock rack; The Mountaineers' guided trips to this peak also require crevasse-rescue proficiency and standard glacier gear.
what_to_bring: glacier rope + crevasse-rescue kit (harness, prusiks/Tibloc, pulley, locking biners)
overnight camping/bivy gear (most parties do this as a 2-day trip with a camp at Diobsud Lakes or a saddle on the Diobsud Creek Glacier)

detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is used on the standard North Ridge route — this is an unroped scramble, not a roped climb. No cams, nuts, or slings are placed. Parties describe the route as forested ridge travel with brush, a short crampon-and-helmet bypass gully around a cliff band near 5,400 ft, and an exposed summit ledge traverse — none involve gear placements.
pro_needs: None — no fixed or removable protection is used. The only protective gear is a helmet for the loose-rock cliff-bypass gully (~5,400 ft) and traction (ice axe + crampons/microspikes) for lingering snow on the upper ridge, which can persist into summer on north-facing slopes.
what_to_bring: microspikes or crampons for spring/early-summer snow
plenty of water — no reliable water source on the north ridge

detailed_rack: No rock rack is needed. In snow season, carry an ice axe per person and consider light aluminum crampons or microspikes for a firm morning gully; some parties bring a short rope or 30m cord to belay or hand-line the steep snow headwall below the notch, and a picket if the party includes less experienced members. In dry season no technical gear is required at all beyond a helmet, which is genuinely worth wearing in the loose gully.
pro_needs: None in the technical sense — there is no protectable rock climbing on this route. The only 'protection' decision is whether to rope or hand-line the steep snow headwall in the gully below the notch in spring conditions, which parties are reported doing.
what_to_bring: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass for the trailhead
3 L water (there is no water above the lower creek crossings)
offline map/GPX and a compass — the traverse below the cliff bands is the crux of the navigation
gloves for the brush, roots and snow
sun protection for the open upper basin
bear awareness — make noise on the forested path

detailed_rack: A trad rack to about 3 inches covers the low-angle slab moves and the 3-pitch 5.6+ summit block; many parties simul-climb or solo the low-angle slab in approach shoes and only rope up near the top.
pro_needs: Protection on the slab itself is thin and infrequent — expect long run-outs on clean, low-angle stone; gear placements become more standard on the summit-block pitches.
what_to_bring: approach shoes or trail runners for most of the slab
rock shoes for the final summit chimney/block
full water supply for the day (no water on the slab)
light camp gear for the ~12-mile approach

detailed_rack: Ten stoppers, two small cams, and six runners were adequate for the whole route on one recorded ascent. A single 50m rope is enough for the rappels, but 60m or two 50m ropes let 3-person parties reach belay stances more comfortably. Rock shoes recommended for the summit block.
pro_needs: Protection is minimal but adequate — small cams and stoppers protect the crack/dihedral pitch. The crux first pitch has marginal protection near an old, loose piton in broken rock; extra care is warranted there.
what_to_bring: Northwest Forest Pass / interagency pass for trailhead parking
Free self-issue wilderness permit (available at trailhead)
Multi-day backpacking/camping kit for the approach
Approach shoes for talus and gully scrambling

detailed_rack: A trad rack to about 3 inches covers the sparse 4th/low-5th slab moves and the 3-pitch 5.6+ summit block; many parties simul-climb or solo the low-angle slab in approach shoes and only rope up near the top.
pro_needs: Protection on the slab itself is thin and infrequent — expect long run-outs on clean, low-angle stone; gear placements become more standard on the summit-block pitches.
what_to_bring: approach shoes or trail runners for most of the slab
rock shoes for the final summit chimney/block
full water supply for the day (no water on the slab)
light camp gear for the ~12-mile approach

detailed_rack: No technical rack is needed. This is an unroped Grade II scramble (river crossing, forest/brush route-finding, snow slopes, and a short Class 2-3 rock section) — no cams, nuts, or protection are placed any
pro_needs: Minimal technical gear - this is a scramble, but the cliff-band crux around 4,900-5,100 ft has real exposure and is sometimes protected with a rope and a couple of pieces by less experienced or larger parties, especially when wet or icy.
what_to_bring: ice axe (snow lingers on the crux band into June-July)
crampons if snow is icy on the cliff band
navigation (GPS/map) - the boot path is easy to lose above treeline
gloves and sturdy pants/gaiters for devil's club and brush
headlamp - full days often run 8-11 hours car-to-car

detailed_rack: No technical rack is used on this route. The only detailed trip report of an actual Berdeen Peak ascent (a Mystery Ridge enchainment approaching via Porkbelly Ridge and the east side/NW slopes) describes mostly Class 3 terrain with one or two Class 4 moves on steep, mossy, loose rock, and does not mention a rope, harness, or any protection being placed or carried for the summit scramble itself.
pro_needs: None needed — this is an unroped Class 3-4 scramble. The limiting factor is loose, mossy rock and careful hold selection, not a lack of protectable terrain, so gear is a non-issue; a helmet is the main protective item worth carrying given the reported rockfall/handhold-failure hazard.
what_to_bring: sturdy boots or scrambling shoes with good traction on wet/mossy rock
ice axe if snow lingers in approach gullies (seasonal)
map/compass or GPS — off-trail, unmaintained route on a peak described as 'not climbed often'
trekking poles for the Porkbelly Ridge bushwhack approach
overnight/camping gear if basing at Berdeen Lake as most parties do

detailed_rack: No roped rack is needed for the standard line — this is an unroped scramble. A helmet is effectively mandatory given the loose rock; some parties carry an ice axe for lingering early-season snow on the approach slopes.
pro_needs: No rack or fixed protection is used on this route — it is unroped Class 2-3 talus and scree scrambling up the SE ridge (from Copper Glance/Eightmile Pass), not technical rock climbing. Parties describe the rock as generally solid on larger blocks but covered in loose 'kitty litter' talus/scree, so the primary hazard is rockfall/footing rather than lack of protection. No party is known to have placed gear or used a rope.
what_to_bring: ice axe (carry if early-season snow lingers in the approach gullies/couloirs)
crampons (situational — only needed if steep snow is encountered; one trip report carried but rarely used them)
sun protection (long, mostly open talus/scree approach)
extra water (long approach, ~11.6 mi round trip with ~5,600 ft gain)
overnight/camp gear if doing Big + West Craggy together (commonly a 2-day trip)
navigation (GPS/map/compass) — off-trail travel above Eightmile Pass/Copper Glance basin

detailed_rack: A light rock rack plus a 60m rope for the descent rappel; full steep-snow kit (ice axe, crampons) for winter/spring couloir conditions.
pro_needs: Protection is minimal and often not encountered until the descent rappel anchor; the route is more about steep, exposed scrambling/snow-climbing than sustained gear placements.
what_to_bring: Current NWAC avalanche forecast for winter/spring ascents
GPS and backup map -- route-finding through the basin is reported as difficult even by experienced parties
Full rope length margin for the south-ridge rappel
Insect protection (wasp nests reported in the lower basin)

detailed_rack: A moderate rock rack to 5.7, plus rappel gear for the inter-tower notch and an ice axe/crampons for the summit snowfield.
pro_needs: Standard trad rack sufficient for 5.7 terrain on the towers; the crux is more about route-finding and commitment across three towers than sustained hard climbing.
what_to_bring: Extra rappel tat/anchor material for the notch

detailed_rack: None needed — the standard route is a non-technical class 2-3 scramble; trip reports (including a winter ascent) note the party carried no rope. An ice axe may be prudent if snow lingers on the approach slopes early in the season.
pro_needs: No protection is placed on this route. It is an unroped Class 2-3 scramble: talus and scree up to the ridge, then a class 2 ridge walk with one or two class 3 moves through loose rock near the summit's distinctive black hornfels cap. Rock quality on the cap itself is described as solid but the approach slopes/gullies are loose — a helmet is the main protective item recommended, not a rack. No trip report reviewed (from either the NE-ridge/Shellrock Pass side or the east Monument Creek basin side) mentions placing gear.
what_to_bring: water treatment/extra capacity — fill at Eureka Creek, upper basin tarns are unreliable/seasonal
map/compass or GPS — remote Pasayten cross-country route-finding on talus, no maintained trail on the peak itself
early start to avoid afternoon heat on exposed ridge
layers — exposed alpine ridge, weather can change fast in the Pasayten

detailed_rack: Bring a double set of cams from #0.5 to #3 (emphasis on #1-2.5), a set of nuts covering small to large sizes, and large hexes. A single 60- or 70-meter rope is all you need; most of the route is simul-climbed and the descent is a walk-off. Approach shoes or light boots work well; approach is mostly 3rd class scrambling on talus.
pro_needs: Protection is generally moderate throughout the route. Rock quality in the initial gully is poor with limited reliable placements; two fixed pins are reportedly on the first pitch but are often missed by parties. The crux section features downsloping, awkward terrain with limited protection. Rock quality improves substantially on the ridge crest where solid placements become more available. Most climbers simul-climb the middle and upper sections, requiring efficient rope management rather than multiple belayed pitches.
what_to_bring: Three season or light four-season jacket

detailed_rack: A light alpine rock rack (set of nuts, cams to roughly 3 inches) for the class 4-5 rib, plus glacier travel gear (axe, crampons, and consider pickets/screws) for the approach glacier and icefall traverse.
pro_needs: Standard trad protection for the class 4-5 rib climbing; extra care placing protection in the crumbly red stratum band at mid-height, which the first-ascent party specifically noted as looser than the otherwise sound surrounding rock.
what_to_bring: Bivy/camping gear for the multi-day approach
Extra care/gear for the icefall crossing (may warrant a rope even on the approach)

detailed_rack: A single rack of cams (small to #2) plus some nuts and pickets is the documented kit; on the first winter ascent, pitons and hexes proved more reliable than cams in icy cracks, and buried ski poles served as deadman anchors.
pro_needs: Mixed snow/ice/rock protection: cams and nuts for rock, pickets for snow, with pitons/hexes preferred over cams in icy or rimed cracks.
what_to_bring: Skis or snowshoes for the winter approach
Rime/ice-clearing tool if attempting in icy conditions
Extra insulation — the face and summit ridge are wind-exposed

detailed_rack: No technical rack is needed for the standard summer condition — this is an unroped Class 2-3 scree/talus scramble. In early season (typically before mid-to-late July), carry an ice axe and crampons for the snow-covered south face and the corniced final ridge.
pro_needs: None for the summer scramble condition; no fixed protection exists on this route. Early-season ascents crossing the corniced east ridge/gendarmes near the Fernow-Buckskin saddle are a genuine mountaineering undertaking and should be treated with full glacier-travel judgment.
what_to_bring: trekking poles for the long approach

detailed_rack: Helmet; 60m rope x2 (doubles strongly preferred for the 5-rappel descent — single-rope parties need an intermediate anchor at the big ledge); full nut set; cams to 4 inches (a #4-equivalent placed a few times on route); about 10 alpine draws; rock shoes. Consider doubling 0.5–1 in cams if 5.8 is near your limit.
pro_needs: Solid alpine rock pro across the grade; some natural placements.
what_to_bring: bivy gear if camping at The Bench or Burgundy Col

detailed_rack: This is an unroped scramble with no fixed protection; a rope, harness, and rack are not standard for the summer route. In early season (typically through June), carry an ice axe and consider crampons for the persistent snow in the summit gully and on north-facing sections. A helmet is recommended given loose rock and the possibility of parties above.
what_to_bring: mountain bike (optional, speeds the Monte Cristo approach)

detailed_rack: No technical rock gear is used; this is an entirely unroped scramble. In early season, some parties carry a lightweight ice axe and traction for the Coney Lake snow-couloir variation.
pro_needs: None on the standard summer line; an ice axe and crampons only if using the early-season snow-couloir variation around the towers.
what_to_bring: extra water (dry ridge and bowl traverse)
wind layers for the exposed traverse
Enchantment core-zone permit if using the descent-loop option and camping

detailed_rack: No technical rock gear is needed. An ice axe is worthwhile early in the season for snow on the upper slopes, and trekking poles help on the long talus.
pro_needs: There is no protectable climbing on the standard route; this is unroped scrambling. The challenge is navigation and stamina rather than gear.

detailed_rack: Primarily an unroped scramble. Carry a helmet for rockfall/loose rock, plus an ice axe and crampons for the snow gully and saddle traverse through at least early July. A light rack (a few small cams/nuts and slings) and a 30m rope are worth carrying for the short technical step guarding the true summit, though most parties simply downclimb it unroped.
pro_needs: No fixed protection reported. Any gear carried is only for the optional short technical step below the true summit, on sound granodiorite/quartz diorite.
what_to_bring: map and compass/GPS — the route above camp is unmarked and there's no official GPX
extra water — the basin camp is typically the last reliable water source
overnight/bivy gear for the high camp
ice axe and crampons if climbing in May or June

detailed_rack: Ice axe and crampons for the CJ Couloir (may not be needed on the chimney itself if it's dry). For the NW Chimney: a single rack of nuts plus something wide — a Big Bro or a large cam — for the loose 5-6" crux crack; a 2013 ascent party carried only 7-8 nuts and found solid placements scarce on the first pitch. Bring 60m doubles so you can build and rappel full-length off your own anchors back to the moat; there are no fixed rap stations on this route.
pro_needs: Protection on the NW Chimney is sparse and the rock is loose and broken; the crux pitch offers only a couple of solid nut placements in a wide, rotten crack, so a large cam or Big Bro helps. There are no established rappel anchors anywhere on the route — plan to build your own on the way down and expect to leave some gear behind.
what_to_bring: single rack of nuts plus a wide piece (Big Bro/large cam)
avalanche beacon, shovel, probe for the couloir approach

detailed_rack: Published descriptions specify medium rock protection up to 4+ inches, runners and a helmet. In practice: a single set of nuts, cams from small through 4 inches (with the larger sizes for the left-facing corner and the left-leaning crack), and a generous set of alpine draws and double-length runners for slinging blocks and horns and for keeping drag manageable on a wandering line. Two ropes, or one 60m plus a tag, so that bailing from the middle of the route is possible. Spare slings and rap rings. A helmet is explicitly called for.
pro_needs: The route is rated PG13. The crux third pitch — the vertical crack in the left-facing corner — is described as well protected and is the best pitch on the climb; the problem is the short second pitch of scary, unstable Class 4+ rock leading to it, where the protection and the rock quality are both poor. The short 5.9+ left-leaning crack higher up is the other place where gear matters. Elsewhere the rock eases and the climbing is moderate. Sling solid features in preference to placing cams in the fractured andesite.
what_to_bring: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass
free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit
approach shoes to cache below the east face
Beckey's Cascade Alpine Guide (or a photo of the Northeast Ridge approach description)
warm layers and a wind shell for a shaded aspect
insect repellent or headnet before mid-July

detailed_rack: Minimal. A short rope, a few nuts and cams to 3 inches for the chimney and any belays you decide to build, and half a dozen long runners for slinging chockstones and horns. A rappel device and a couple of spare slings and rap rings to replace or back up the fixed anchor near the top. Helmets throughout — the couloir funnels everything the upper mountain sheds. Early in the season, an ice axe and crampons, since this aspect stays snow-filled.
pro_needs: The route is Class 3, so most parties move unroped over most of it, but the chockstone chimney and the upper friction slab are the two places where a rope is worth having, and the slab in particular offers very little to place — the large flake used as a handrail is the main feature. Slinging chockstones in the couloir gives the most reliable anchors on this rock.
what_to_bring: Helmet (critical given the documented rockfall accident here)
Rope/rappel device if descending past the chockstone

detailed_rack: Light alpine rock rack: small nuts, cams from about 0.2 to 2 in (a #3 optional), several single- and double-length slings, a cordelette for anchors at ledges, plus extra webbing and rap rings for the descent anchors. Carry an ice axe if snow lingers.
pro_needs: Protection is good on pitch 1 (chimney/crack) but sparse and runout on pitch 2's traverse, where placements can be more than 50 ft apart; the upper 3rd/4th-class terrain takes little gear. Build solid anchors at stances with a cordelette and slings.
what_to_bring: Approach shoes or light boots for the talus/scramble approach
Extra webbing/rap rings for descent anchors
Ice axe if snow lingers in the approach basin
Trekking poles for the approach trail

detailed_rack: A few ice screws (3-4), 2-3 pickets, slings for frequent tree-anchor belays on P2/P3, and a couple of small rock pieces or pitons for the crux step; two tools and crampons are mandatory.
pro_needs: Screws, pickets, and a few rock pieces for the mixed step(s).

detailed_rack: A 60m rope and a medium alpine rack; light crampons and a light ice axe are recommended into early summer.
pro_needs: The first 15m into the entrance couloir has no protection but stays moderate; good protection resumes on the 5.7 climbing to the ridge crest. A loose chockstone low on the route and a poorly protected 10 ft headwall are specific noted concerns.
what_to_bring: Light crampons and axe for early-season snow/glide cracks on the approach
Extra care around the loose lower chockstone

detailed_rack: No fixed rock protection is documented as necessary; the summit scramble is unroped Class 3 on loose rock. Crampons and an ice axe are recommended for the Pilz Glacier traverse; a rope and basic crevasse-rescue kit are prudent given the glacier's crevassing.
pro_needs: Glacier travel kit (rope, crevasse-rescue gear) for the Pilz Glacier margin; no technical rock protection is used on the standard scramble line.
what_to_bring: Full backpacking/camp kit for a 2-3 day trip
Bug protection for the Napeequa Valley camp
Sun protection for exposed alpine slab traverses

detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard line. Parties carry a single ice axe and crampons for the snow sections above Chalangin Basin, plus a helmet for the loose cliff band around 5,500-6,500 ft. A rope and light crevasse-rescue kit are prudent only if a variation strays onto the crevassed margin of the Pilz Glacier.
pro_needs: Standard glacier/steep-snow protection (ice axe, crampons); no fixed or removable rock protection is documented as necessary on the standard south-slope/southwest-face line.
what_to_bring: Water-crossing shoes or sandals for Thunder Creek
Bivy/camp gear if splitting the trip into 2-3 days
Bug protection for the Thunder Creek bushwhack in summer

detailed_rack: 9 quickdraws, 30m+ rope, helmet.
pro_needs: Bolts to a shared chain anchor; standard sport rack.
what_to_bring: rock shoes (precision fit recommended for the thin seams)

detailed_rack: Single rack of cams to #4 Camalot with doubles in the offwidth-prone sizes (#0.75, #1, #2, #3 or equivalent), a set of nuts, 12-16 slings, two 60m ropes for the rappels, and a helmet.
pro_needs: Solid alpine trad rack with doubles through offwidth sizes (#0.75-#3); comfort placing and evaluating gear in wide cracks and on fixed rappel anchors.
what_to_bring: rock shoes roomy enough to jam (offwidth sections)
ice axe and crampons (early season, for the Burgundy Col traverse)
headlamp for an early alpine start

detailed_rack: No published rack exists for this specific line, so carry the standard Chianti east-face kit: a set of nuts, doubles of cams from finger size through #3 Camalot, and a #3.5 or #4 Camalot for the offwidth the first-ascent party describes low on the route. Add 8-10 alpine draws and several double-length slings for the long left-leaning ramp, which will generate rope drag. Two 60 m ropes are essential for the descent and for the option of escaping onto Rebel Yell's rappel line. Ice axe and crampons for the approach traverse round out the kit.
pro_needs: Standard alpine trad protection on granite: ramps, a left-facing corner and an offwidth, with no fixed gear reported on the line itself. The offwidth section will want at least one large cam. Because the route crosses Rebel Yell, the fixed anchors on that line (bolts at the top of P4 and at both ends of the P5 offwidth, plus the two-bolt station at the base of the summit block) are usable for retreat. Expect more lichen and less-travelled rock than on Rebel Yell - the route's name is a fair warning - so protect for the possibility of a loose hold.
what_to_bring: Trekking poles for the steep sandy approach and descent
2-3 L water capacity - the bench spring and snow at Burgundy Col are the only sources
Long sleeves and trousers for the offwidth and lichen
Sunglasses, sun hat, high-SPF sunscreen for snow glare
Wind shell and a light insulating layer
Bivy or camping kit if overnighting; stove to melt snow at the col
Map and compass or GPS on the Silver Star Mountain quad
A photo of the east face taken from the approach traverse to help identify the ramp

detailed_rack: A standard single alpine rack to 3 inches covers the 5.6 climbing: a set of nuts, cams from about 0.4 to 3 inches, and 6-8 alpine draws plus a couple of double-length slings for the blocky north-face features. Two 60 m ropes are the norm in the Wine Spires because every descent option in the group is rappel-based and 60 m doubles let you leave the mountain from anywhere. Add an ice axe and aluminium crampons for the col gully and the traverse beneath Burgundy's east face - these are on the list all season, not just in spring.
pro_needs: Historically protected with pitons; a modern ascent would rack a standard light alpine trad rack given the moderate 5.6 grade, but no contemporary route description was found to confirm current gear beta.
what_to_bring: Trekking poles (repeatedly called the most important gear in the Wine Spires for the sandy descent)
2-3 L water capacity - the bench spring and Burgundy Col snow are the only reliable sources
Sun hat, sunglasses and high-SPF sunscreen for snow glare
Wind/rain shell and an insulating layer for the shaded north face
Gaiters for the scree and snow
Bivy gear if camping at the col; a stove to melt snow
Map and compass or GPS with the Silver Star Mountain quad
Small first-aid kit and blister care

detailed_rack: No technical rack is needed on the standard Class 2-3 line; bring an ice axe (light traction optional) for firm snow on the approach and near the col into early-mid summer. A rope/small rack only comes into play if combining with Fortress Mountain's Class 3-4 east ridge, or if you stray off the cairned line into the low-5th-class gully some parties have mistakenly followed.
pro_needs: Non-technical Class 2-3 scramble on the standard line; an ice axe covers firm snow on the approach and col through early-mid summer. No rope, rack, or crevasse-rescue gear is needed on this side of the mountain unless you detour onto the glaciated NE (Lyman Glacier) side or add Fortress Mountain's Class 3-4 east ridge.

detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed; this is a glacier scramble rather than a roped rock climb. Bring a standard glacier-travel kit — ice axe, crampons, a rope for the team, and a basic crevasse-rescue rack (a few ice screws, prusik cords or mechanical ascenders, a pulley, and slings/carabiners) for the Walrus Glacier crossing, where narrow crevasses and at least one snow-bridge are typically encountered.
pro_needs: Glacier-travel and crevasse-rescue gear rather than rock protection: a rope, crevasse-rescue hardware, ice axe, and crampons for the glacier chute. No fixed or removable rock protection is typically placed on the Class 3 scrambling sections above the glacier.
what_to_bring: trekking poles for Boulder Creek fords

detailed_rack: A general glacier kit: ice axe, crampons, a 30 to 60m glacier rope, a couple of pickets, a small crevasse-rescue kit, and a helmet. No rock gear is needed for the standard line.
pro_needs: Protection is limited to pickets in the steeper snow near the col and standard glacier-travel anchors. The summit rocks are low-class scrambling and take no gear.
rack: 30-60m glacier rope for a 2-person rope team
Crevasse-rescue kit (pulley, prusiks, screw-gate biners) per rope team

detailed_rack: 60 m rope; 8-10 ice screws (most racked for the short crux pitch, including a couple of stubbies); 2 ice tools each; a few pickets; a light rock rack (small cams/nuts, maybe a pin) for anchors in the poor-quality summit rock; V-thread hardware for a retreat.
pro_needs: 8-10 ice screws (concentrated on the crux pitch), a few pickets, and a light rock rack/pin for belay anchors in poor rock; V-thread hardware for a retreat.

detailed_rack: 60 m rope; 10+ ice screws (several stubbies) concentrated for the WI6 crux pitch; V-thread/Abalakov hardware; 2 technical ice tools; a couple of pickets for the upper snowfield; extra slings/cord for tat at existing anchors.
pro_needs: 10+ ice screws weighted toward the WI6 crux pitch, V-thread/Abalakov hardware, and a couple of pickets for the upper snowfield; a rock rack is not typically needed.

detailed_rack: No roped gear is required for the standard ascent in good summer conditions - it's an off-trail alpine scramble. Carry an ice axe and crampons or microspikes for any lingering snow/ice on the exposed traverse below the summit, especially in early or late season. A short rope and a few slings are worth carrying as a security option for the class 4 chimney/crack move and the summit cliff-band bypass, though most parties climb the route unroped.
pro_needs: Essentially none for the standard summer scramble; any rope/slings carried are for optional security at the class 4 move and cliff band, not for sustained protection.
what_to_bring: mountain bike (optional — saves significant time on the flat Monte Cristo Road)

detailed_rack: Most parties climb this as an unroped scramble, carrying an ice axe and crampons for the snowfield below the ridge. A light rack (a few slings, a 30m rope) is worth having for the short, exposed class 4 moves near the summit notches, where some parties prefer to belay rather than solo them.
pro_needs: A light rack (a few slings and small cams/nuts) covers the short exposed class 4 step; most parties otherwise scramble the class 3 sections unroped in good conditions and only rope up for the glacier/snowfield crossing.
rack: 30m rope for the crossing and an optional belay
A few slings + small cams/nuts for the exposed class 4 step (optional)
what_to_bring: navigation tools (map/compass/GPS - route is unmarked past the Copper Creek Trail)
satellite communicator (no cell coverage in the Railroad Creek drainage)
water treatment and sun protection for the long glacier-basin approach
cash/reservation confirmation for the Holden Village shuttle

detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is typically needed - the standard route is a Class 3-4 scramble, not a roped rock climb. Most parties carry crampons and an axe for the Lewis Glacier crossing plus a single 30 m rope, a few slings, and rap rings to protect or rappel the short steep snow/rock step below the ridge notch.
pro_needs: Primarily a glacier-approach scramble: crampons and an axe for the Lewis Glacier, plus a light rope for optional protection/rappel of the short steep step near the ridge notch. No rack or free-climbing gear is typically required for the Class 3-4 terrain above.

detailed_rack: The standard route is an unroped scramble for experienced parties in good conditions, so no traditional rack is used; carry an ice axe (and crampons if snow is firm, or for glacier variants such as approaches via the Mesahchie/Katsuk glaciers), plus a helmet for the loose talus and 3rd-class rock. Some parties carry a rope and a light rack/slings for the final rock step or for crevasse rescue on glaciated variants, though it is not required for the standard south-side ridge route in typical late-summer conditions.
pro_needs: Typically scrambled unroped on 3rd-class rock; a rope/light rack is rarely carried but can help on the exposed 4th-class Kimtah–Cosho connecting ridge if linking the two peaks.

detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is used on the standard route; it is climbed as an unroped scramble. Some parties carry a light rope/harness for the crux gully as a personal safety margin, particularly for less-experienced scramblers or in wet conditions.
pro_needs: None required for the standard line; it is not a protected/roped route. An ice axe may be prudent in early season if snow lingers in the gully or on the upper slopes.
what_to_bring: Wilderness permit (self-issue at Canyon Creek Trailhead)
Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent for trailhead parking
Water treatment (Crater Lake and creek crossings are the water sources)
Extra layers — exposed ridge and summit are wind-prone

detailed_rack: A standard glacier-travel rack rather than a rock rack: one rope per rope team, harnesses for all climbers, 2-3 pickets and/or ice screws for crevasse-rescue anchors and to belay the short summit moat crossing, ice axes, crampons, and helmets. A basic crevasse-rescue kit (prusik cords or mechanical ascenders, a pulley, extra slings and locking carabiners) should be carried by each rope team. Little to no traditional rock protection is used on the standard line; the final scrambling is generally unroped in good conditions.
pro_needs: Protection needs on this route are glacier-travel oriented rather than rock-gear oriented: pickets or ice screws for crevasse-rescue anchors and a body or picket belay for the short, exposed moat/bergschrund crossing onto the summit ridge are the main technical protection used; the summit scramble itself is typically climbed unroped.
what_to_bring: Bug repellent and long sleeves (brushy approach)
Bear-resistant food storage per wilderness regulations

detailed_rack: Rack used on the 2005 ascent: a full set of wires, knifeblades, lost arrows, and Friends/cams from #1 to #3.5, plus a picket would have been useful. Add a few short and medium ice screws — stubbies specifically, since the useful placements were in thin ice under an overhang and in the ice above the chockstone — a single rope, two technical ice tools and crampons. The pitons are not optional: the rock is compact and the knifeblades proved their worth on the runout bulge below the chockstone. Belays were improvised from a cam, a stubby screw and a doubtful horn. Bring slings and tat for rappel anchors you may have to leave behind.
pro_needs: Poor to marginal throughout. The lower band is compact gneiss and was simul-climbed with long gaps between pieces; the crux traverse across a partially iced slab is terrain where a leader cannot afford to fall. Pins are the primary protection. The one properly protected move on the route is the chockstone itself — a cam below the roof and a stubby screw in the good ice on the left. On the upper couloir and rib, expect simul-climbing with occasional gear and very large exposure. Nothing about this route rewards a cam-only rack.
what_to_bring: Compass and USGS 7.5' Diablo Dam quad — the descent timber is too thick to see the dam lights, and a bearing error puts you back in Stetattle Creek
Headlamp with spare batteries; the 2005 party credited a bright headlamp with saving them repeatedly
Altimeter or GPS — Beckey's stated couloir-top elevation is wrong by roughly 500 ft
Footwear or a plan for the Stetattle Creek ford
Water carry for the south-side descent, which is dry
Light bivouac gear, stove and no-cook backup
North Cascades wilderness permit for the overnight
Shuttle-car keys — the climb finishes four road miles from the approach trailhead

detailed_rack: Very little. One winter party carried no rock protection and no ice screws at all, using occasional ice-axe belays, and was roped for much of the trip above the saddle; they carried snowshoes to the 5,720+ ft saddle and left them there for the summit climb. For a spring or summer ascent, a light rope, a handful of nuts and a few slings covers the 200 ft of slab above the saddle if it turns out to be bare or wet — nobody has published what that slab actually takes in dry conditions, and the author of that account explicitly asks for that information. An ice axe is the essential item in any season with snow, and crampons for a firm morning on the upper slopes.
pro_needs: Effectively none on the standard line. The protection question is confined to Beckey's 200 ft of slab above the saddle and the short steep step onto the ridge; in snow both are handled with an axe and, at most, an axe belay. Bare-rock beta for that section has never been published. Treat a rope, a few nuts and slings as contingency rather than as a working rack, and be prepared to make the call at the saddle.
what_to_bring: Water, 2-4 L — the entire route faces south and has no source once the snow is gone
USGS 7.5' Diablo Dam quad plus compass; an altimeter genuinely improves your odds on the outcrops
Sun protection and light long sleeves — full south aspect, all day
Gaiters and durable trousers for salal and slide alder
Trekking poles for 6,000 ft of steep descent
Headlamp with spare batteries; the descent runs long
Wilderness permit if you camp at the saddle
Bivy or tent capable of a snow ledge if going overnight in winter — one party recorded -22F at the saddle

detailed_rack: No technical rack; ice axe useful for lingering snow in the basin and on the approach switchbacks early season. Helmet strongly recommended above Foggy Lake due to rockfall from parties on the scramble.
pro_needs: None.
what_to_bring: sturdy approach shoes with good friction for the granite scramble
sun protection (basin and summit are fully exposed)

detailed_rack: Not a roped climb for most parties; an ice axe and crampons are the primary tools for the snow slopes, and some parties carry a short sling/handline as backup on the cable-protected ledge below the summit.
pro_needs: No fixed protection beyond the resort-installed steel cable on the final ledge; a rope is not typically used but could be carried for extra security on that section.

detailed_rack: A single rack of cams to 3 inches (e.g. doubles from 0.5-2 with a 3 and small tricams per one party's report) and a single 60m rope covers the technical pitches; bring crampons and an ice axe (or two tools) for the glacier approach and any firm snow on the ridge.
pro_needs: Protection is thin and sometimes suspect on the lower 5.5 pitch off the col — test every placement to ensure it's attached to the mountain; gear improves and cracks are better higher up on the two 5.7 pitches near the summit.
what_to_bring: Rock shoes for the crux pitches
Overnight camp gear for the Eldorado high camp
Sun protection for extended glacier travel
NPS wilderness backcountry permit (fee applies in summer)

detailed_rack: No technical rack needed; an axe, crampons, and optionally a short rope/picket for the exposed summit-pinnacle traverse.
pro_needs: No technical protection needed for the couloir itself; optional light rack (nuts/small cams) only if attempting the 5.6 summit-pinnacle variation.

detailed_rack: No rack used; treated as an unroped scramble. An ice axe is useful for early-season snow on the upper ridge.
what_to_bring: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful Pass
footwear/poles suited to repeated creek crossings
layers for the exposed upper ridge

detailed_rack: Medium-sized rock climbing rack: 1-2x each of 0.5-1.5 inch cams, medium stopper set, 2-3 slings, 2-3 quickdraws, ice tools and crampons if early season or water ice present, single 50-60m rope sufficient for climbing, 2x 50m ropes for rappelling.
pro_needs: Full trad protection on well-formed cracks and pockets. Most placements are solid granite with good rock quality. Anchors can be built with cams and slings; no fixed anchors present. Rappel anchors should be redundant with bomber placements.

detailed_rack: Light rack to 3 inches: approach shoes and medium pack for approach, 1-2 sets of quickdraws for potential fixed anchors, single set of traditional cams (0.5-3"), supplemented with small wired nuts (RZA or similar), 4-6 slings of various lengths, two 60m dynamic ropes (single strand rated), rescue pulley and friction device for rappel safety, belay device, locking carabiners.
pro_needs: Light traditional rock rack through 3 inches. Natural protection abundant from granite flakes and crack systems, but Pitch 2 includes a 25-30 foot dyke section with limited pro. Two 60m ropes required for two-rappel descent. Sling and carabiner anchor kit essential. No ice tools required on standard East Face route.
rack: Light cam rack 0.5–3in + small wired nuts
what_to_bring: Water bottles or hydration pack (3L minimum)

detailed_rack: A light alpine rack — small set of nuts/cams to about 2 inches, a few slings — plus ice axe and crampons for the glacier and snow gully, and a rope for the low-5th-class ridge traverse and any short rappels.
pro_needs: Gear needs are modest: mostly for the short 5.6 sections on the connecting ridge and summit block, since the bulk of the route is snow/glacier travel and 3rd-4th class scrambling.
rack: Rope (~30m sufficient) for the ridge traverse/short rappels
what_to_bring: ice axe and crampons for the approach and col gully
navigation (map/compass/GPS) — no maintained trail past the Terror Creek junction
overnight/bivy kit for the Terror Basin camp
bear canister (free loaners available at the Wilderness Information Center)
satellite communicator — no cell coverage in the Pickets
trekking poles for the brushy, blowdown-choked lower approach

detailed_rack: None -- an unroped Class 2-3 scramble; no rope, rack, or crampons typically needed once the trail and ridge are snow-free. Carry an ice axe into early summer for lingering snow patches/cornices near the summit block.
pro_needs: None — an unroped Class 2-3 scramble; no rack or rope is typically carried.
what_to_bring: Ice axe (useful into early summer for lingering snow near the summit)
Helmet for loose rock on the ridge
Light bivy kit if overnighting at 6,300 ft or 6,900 ft
Map/compass or GPS -- the flagged climbers' trail is easy to lose off-route

detailed_rack: A standard alpine rock rack for sustained 5.9 face/chimney/arête climbing, plus glacier travel gear (crampons, axe, rope) for the Mustard Glacier approach.
A standard glacier kit: ice axe, crampons, a 30 to 60m glacier rope, a couple of pickets, a crevasse-rescue kit, and a helmet. No rock gear is needed.
pro_needs: Protection is limited to pickets on the summit arête and standard glacier-travel anchors. The route is about snow and glacier skills rather than rock protection.

detailed_rack: Ice axe plus a second tool for the steeper sections, crampons, a few ice screws, a couple of pickets, and a glacier rope with rescue kit.
pro_needs: The couloir takes pickets and the occasional screw where ice forms; the glacier uses standard travel anchors. Protection is sparse, so confident steep-snow technique is essential.

detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is used on this scramble — it is unroped class 2-3 terrain for essentially all parties. A helmet is recommended given the loose rock reported on the upper gully and rock rib.
pro_needs: None — this is an unroped scramble route; a rope is not carried by documented parties.

detailed_rack: No technical rack — unroped class 3 scrambling. A helmet is prudent given the loose, erosion-carved rock.
pro_needs: None — rope is not used by documented parties on this line.
what_to_bring: map/GPS for the off-trail gully section
overnight camp gear if approaching via Emerald Park
sun protection for the exposed summit slab

detailed_rack: No technical rock gear is needed for the standard scramble. An ice axe is worth carrying early in the season for snow on shaded benches, and trekking poles ease the talus.
pro_needs: There is no protectable climbing on the easiest line; movement is unroped scrambling. The demands are basic route-finding and comfort on exposed third-class blocks rather than any gear.

detailed_rack: No technical rack is needed for Fifth of July Mountain's standard south-ridge line; it is class 2 talus/boulder scrambling. A helmet is recommended for loose rock. Parties who detour to bag neighboring Devils Smoke Stack (class 3, with short, exposed steps) may want a short length of rope for confidence, but it is not used on Fifth of July itself.
pro_needs: None — this is an unroped scramble on the standard route.
what_to_bring: ice axe if attempting before early July
helmet for loose talus near the summit
sun protection (hat, sunscreen) for the exposed meadows and summit slopes
map/compass or GPS for the unmarked cross-country section above Cow Creek Meadows

detailed_rack: This is an unroped scramble for competent parties: helmet is considered mandatory for anyone other than the party's leader given the loose rock in the gully. Carry an ice axe (and consider light traction) if snow remains in the gully entrance or on the Ida Creek traverse, typically into July. Some parties carry a short (20-30m) rope or hand line strictly to protect the exposed downclimb near the summit notch; no fixed anchors or rappel gear are needed.
pro_needs: Rope and a light rock rack are optional — most parties solo the Class 3-4 terrain unroped, but the exposed ledges near the summit notch may justify protection for less-experienced climbers.

detailed_rack: A single rack of cams from 0.4 to 2 inches, a set of nuts, about 8 alpine draws with doubles for the towers, and a 60m rope. Carry an ice axe and crampons for the snowy approach.
pro_needs: The crest protects well on the steeper steps with cracks and horns, with run-out moderate climbing between. Slinging gendarmes speeds protection on the long ridge.

detailed_rack: Light single rack through hand size, a set of nuts, plus axe and crampons for the approach glacier.
pro_needs: Medium alpine rack; glacier kit for the approach.

detailed_rack: A single rack of cams from 0.4 to 2 inches, a set of nuts, about 8 alpine draws with a couple of doubles, and a 60m rope. Add an ice axe and crampons for the couloir, especially before midsummer.
pro_needs: The crest protects reasonably well with cracks and horns on the steeper steps, with run-out moderate sections between. The couloir takes a picket or two early season; later it is unprotected loose rock.
what_to_bring: rock shoes or sticky approach shoes

detailed_rack: No rack beyond a light alpine kit is typically carried -- ice axe and crampons for the snow crossing to the col, a helmet for the loose gully, and most parties climb the exposed 4th-class summit step unroped; a rope and a few slings can be worthwhile insurance for less experienced scramblers on that final step.
pro_needs: Minimal fixed protection; this is unroped alpine scrambling with one genuinely exposed 4th-class move near the summit.
what_to_bring: Map/compass or GPS for cross-country basin travel

detailed_rack: No roped climbing gear is needed. In snow season, carry an ice axe and crampons for the moderately steep slope below the summit ridge.
pro_needs: No technical protection needed; parties carry an ice axe and crampons for the snow-covered ridge and gully sections common into early July.
what_to_bring: Extra layers for wind on the ridge

detailed_rack: No technical rock gear is needed for the standard scramble line. Carry an ice axe (and crampons if snow lingers on the pass/ridge, common into early summer) — this is not a roped climb for most parties.
pro_needs: No technical protection needed. A helmet is commonly recommended for the loose rock near the summit and on the ridge.
what_to_bring: Wind layer for the exposed summit ridge
Plenty of water — none reliable past Esmeralda Basin

detailed_rack: A light alpine rock rack is sufficient for the single moderate pitch — a small set of cams and a few nuts. The bulk of the gear list for this objective is multi-day approach and glacier/snow travel equipment (rope, axe, crampons) rather than technical rock gear, since the terrain between basins involves lingering snow and short glacier crossings well into summer.
pro_needs: A light rock rack sufficient for 5.6 terrain, plus standard glacier travel gear (axe, crampons, rope) for the glacier, moat and snow ground below the north side of the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col.
rack: Light alpine rock rack to ~3in with extra slings
Ice axe and crampons (early season col approach)

detailed_rack: No technical rock rack; this is a glacier-approach mountaineering line — carry an ice axe, crampons, and a rope, harness and crevasse-rescue kit for glacier travel on Conrad Glacier.
pro_needs: Glacier travel kit (axe, crampons, rope, harness, crevasse-rescue gear) for the Conrad Glacier crossing to the saddle, then boulder/scree/snowfield travel to the summit (Mazamas).
what_to_bring: overnight gear (typically a 2+ day car-to-car trip per Mazamas)

detailed_rack: Ice axe, crampons, and full glacier travel gear (harness, rope, pickets, crevasse-rescue kit); a helmet is strongly advised for the rockfall-exposed traverse below Disappointment Peak.
pro_needs: Standard glacier protection (pickets/screws for crevasse-rescue anchors); no sustained technical rock/ice protection needed on the standard glacier line.

detailed_rack: Per person: ice axe + second tool, crampons, helmet, harness. Per team: 30–60 m rope, 4–6 ice screws, 2–4 pickets, small rock rack (nuts/small cams) and slings for the notch/gendarmes, rappel/V-thread kit.
pro_needs: Mixed: screws and pickets for steep snow/ice, a light rock rack for the Rabbit Ears/notch, plus rappel gear for the notch.

detailed_rack: Rope, crampons, ice axe, pickets, and about 4 ice screws are typically carried for the bergschrund crossing and headwall.
pro_needs: Screws and pickets for the headwall/bergschrund section; standard glacier crevasse-rescue protection below that.

detailed_rack: Glacier rope team: 30–40 m rope, 2–3 pickets, crevasse-rescue kit. Per person: ice axe, crampons, helmet, harness, locking biners.
pro_needs: Glacier protection only — pickets for the steeper upper snow and crevasse zones.

detailed_rack: A standard alpine trad rack for sustained 5.10 crack and face climbing; no bolts or fixed gear exist anywhere on the route, so a full self-sufficient rack (including small-to-mid cams for the sandy, expanding crux crack) plus a helmet is essential.
pro_needs: The route has no fixed protection or bolts; the crux fourth pitch in particular offers poor, marginal placements in an expanding sandy crack, and one ~20-foot section ('the Pitch of Terror') is essentially unprotectable rotten rock.
what_to_bring: overnight camping gear for a Snowy Lakes basecamp
extra water for a long, exposed east-facing pitch day

detailed_rack: A light alpine rock rack (nuts + cams ~0.3-2in) and 60m rope for climbing and rappelling; ice axe and crampons since this north-aspect face can hold snow into the climbing season.

Gear is minimal. Most parties carry a short/light rope (a 30m glacier or 'rad' line is common) purely to protect or rappel the short low-5th-class step at the summit block, plus a sling or two for a hasty rappel anchor. An ice axe (and crampons in early season) is recommended for the Cutthroat/Granite Pass snowfields that can linger into August.
pro_needs: No fixed protection exists on the route; the crux is short enough that many parties simply spot or hip-belay it. A rope, a sling, and a way to build a quick anchor are enough for those who want to protect or rappel the final move.
what_to_bring: Northwest Forest Pass for trailhead parking
overnight backpacking/camping gear for Snowy Lakes
water treatment (lake water available at camp)
bear canister recommended for food storage
layers for exposed, high-elevation ridge walking

detailed_rack: Ice axe and crampons for snow, a light rack for the short rock steps, and a rope for the exposed sections.
pro_needs: Minimal — a light rack and a rope for the summit block and any snow.

detailed_rack: No technical gear; ice axe handy early season for snow above Foggy Lake.
pro_needs: None.

detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard Class 2 line -- it's a steep trail hike followed by an off-trail ridge walk and short talus/rock scramble. Trekking poles are strongly recommended for the steep, eroded trail; carry an ice axe plus microspikes or light crampons in early season or after fresh snow, since the ridge crest holds snow patches well into summer.
pro_needs: No fixed or removable protection is used; the route is unroped Class 2 terrain.
what_to_bring: helmet for loose rock on the ridge crest
map and compass or GPS for off-trail ridge navigation
bear canister (required in Olympic National Park)
sun protection for the long, exposed ridge walk
sturdy boots suited to scree and talus

detailed_rack: This is an unroped scramble, not a technical rope route — no rock rack is needed for the standard West Ridge line. An ice axe and crampons are recommended, and often necessary, for the snow-covered basin and connecting ledge into mid-August. Some parties carry a short rope/harness as a personal safety margin for the exposed ledge traverse, though it is not commonly protected and no fixed anchors are described.
pro_needs: No fixed protection exists on this route. It is Class 2-3 scrambling with one notably exposed, narrow ledge traverse; parties uncomfortable with unprotected exposure sometimes carry a rope to hand-line the ledge crossing, though most climb it unroped.
what_to_bring: Overnight/bivy gear for a 2-3 day trip (most parties do not day-trip from the trailhead)
Sun protection for extended talus/snow travel
Map/compass or GPS — the 7,900 ft notch and connecting ledge are easy to miss in poor visibility

detailed_rack: 18 quickdraws, 70m rope, helmet.
pro_needs: 16 bolts to a chain anchor; this is the longest single pitch in the area, so bring a full rack and a 70m rope.
what_to_bring: 70m rope specifically — shorter ropes won't lower the full route

detailed_rack: Full range of cracks and aid rack recommended: 1-2x each of 0.3-1.5 inch Alien or TC Pro cams, complete medium-sized stopper set, hexes for medium-sized placements, 0.5-1 inch pitons for aid, 2-3 slings of various sizes, 2 ice axes, crampons, ice tools if early season (possible water ice), 2-3 quickdraws, carabiners, prussiks, cordelette for rappel anchors.
pro_needs: Full trad rack required. Splitter cracks on north faces provide excellent natural protection. Anchors are typically solid granite with bomber placements. Rappel anchors should be redundant and well-tested before weighting. No fixed anchors remain on route.
rack: 5-6 slings plus tat/webbing for sparse fixed anchors
Single dynamic rope for climbing; carry two ropes for the rappel descent (per route beta)
what_to_bring: Sun protection (high SPF sunscreen, glacier glasses)

detailed_rack: Mid-size alpine rock rack with 6-8 cams and nuts (mostly cams for Guye's crumbly rock); 60-meter rope minimum (bring two ropes for safe rappel options); full rack of medium to large chocks; several double runners or slings for extending placements around flakes; helmet (mandatory); climbing shoes; approach shoes or boots.
pro_needs: Protection is generally intermittent and poor-quality due to loose flakes and crumbly rock. Many dirt-filled cracks yield marginal placements. Several old fixed pitons remain on the traverse pitch itself. Plan for lots of sling extensions around features rather than clean gear placements. Tree anchors available for rappel.
what_to_bring: Water (minimum 2-3L due to altitude and exposure)
Headlamp (long approach in summer daylight, but plan for changes)

detailed_rack: Deliberately light. An ice axe is mandatory and crampons are required. A picket and a rope are suggested - a 50m is preferred over a 30m - and slung trees provide the occasional belay on the flanks. Rock protection is described as minimal during peak season, so do not plan a rack around it: bring a few slings, a couple of nuts if you want them, and accept that most of this route is climbed with the axe and your feet. A second tool is worth considering for the steepest upper section even though the route is graded as snow rather than ice.
pro_needs: Minimal. A picket, a few slings for trees, and the acceptance that much of the 70-degree upper gully is effectively unprotected.
what_to_bring: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass for the PCT North trailhead
Insulated layers and shell - half the gully never sees sun
Sunglasses and sunscreen for the sunlit half
Map/GPS track for both the Commonwealth and Cave Ridge descents

detailed_rack: Standard sport rack with 10-12 quickdraws, wired stoppers (sizes 1-4), medium nuts (sizes 1-3), 60m rope, belay device, locking carabiners.
pro_needs: Lead climber comfortable on 5.8+ with mixed protection (bolts and natural gear). Solid footwork and crack skills.

detailed_rack: No technical rock or ice gear is needed - this is a hiking/scrambling route. An ice axe (and possibly microspikes) is worth carrying in the shoulder seasons for lingering snow on the approach and summit slopes.
pro_needs: None - the Class 3 summit block is unroped scrambling on generally solid rock with a short, low-exposure crux.
what_to_bring: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass for trailhead parking
Backpacking gear if overnighting at Pass No Pass or Buck Creek Pass
Bear canister or hang recommended for camping
Layers for exposed, weather-changeable high country
Extra water - open meadow slopes have limited sources

detailed_rack: A light alpine rack is typical for this class-IV/low-5th line: a small set of nuts and cams, a few slings/draws, and a lightweight rope for the short technical sections and any rappels off the col; carry an ice axe and crampons for the approach gully and col when snow-covered (common through mid-summer).
pro_needs: Protection needs are modest and intermittent — mostly natural gear placements on broken, blocky rock for short exposed sections rather than sustained crack climbing.
rack: Light alpine rack: small set of nuts and cams
Lightweight rope for short technical sections and rappels off the col
Ice axe and crampons for approach gully/col
what_to_bring: Ice axe (and crampons in early season) for the approach gully and Barrier crossing
Overnight/bivy gear for the Crescent Creek Basin camp

detailed_rack: Not a roped rock climb for most parties in normal conditions; typical kit is an ice axe and crampons for the snow gully sections plus a helmet for rockfall/loose rock (essential given the crumbly pillow basalt). A rope and glacier gear are not needed for the small glacier remnant traverse (no meaningful crevasse hazard reported), but a rope, a few slings, and light rock protection can be prudent for parties wanting to belay short class 3-4 sections or the Gilhooley Tower area in early/lean-snow conditions.
pro_needs: Standard steep-snow-climbing protection: ice axe and often a second tool, crampons, and a helmet; this is an unroped or occasionally short-roped snow climb rather than a pitched, protected route in the trip reports found.
what_to_bring: Wilderness camping permit if overnighting in Royal Basin
Avalanche awareness / current snow conditions check before committing
Navigation tools for the cross-country approach to the couloir base

detailed_rack: Two 30-meter ropes (single-rope rappels, doubled for security), dynamic belay anchors or pickets at rap stations. Ice axe (technical climbing tool essential for step-cutting and self-arrest). Crampons (rigid or semi-rigid, microspikes insufficient). Rock protection: slings for trees (abundant), quickdraws for anchors. Rappel device (ATC-style or equivalent). Helmet (mandatory due to rockfall and ice fall hazard). Ice screws (optional, for belayed pitches if team prefers; not typical for this route).
pro_needs: Protection is tree-based and natural feature slings; climbers typically clip existing rap slings on descent or place slings around large trees. Rock is granodiorite; belay anchors should be bombproof trees or solid rock features. No bolts; this is entirely natural protection and tree anchors.
what_to_bring: Insulated jacket (down or synthetic for winter)
Insulated gloves and inner glove liners
Pack (60-70L for two-day, or 35-40L if dayhike push)
Food and water (2-3 liters carrying capacity)
Map and compass (USGS Mount Index quad)
GPS device or smartphone with offline maps
First aid kit (blister treatment, pain relief)
Avalanche beacon, probe, shovel (for group climbing)

detailed_rack: No rock rack. Ice axe, crampons for the cirque snowfields, helmet, and boots that take crampons. One documented party carried a rope and reported it useless because the rock would not accept protection; if you carry one anyway, keep it to a 30 m line with a few slings for a horn belay over the eroded step.
pro_needs: Essentially none is placeable. Treat the route as a soloing exercise on loose ground - protection comes from movement discipline and conservative decision-making, not gear.
what_to_bring: Passport or NEXUS - the approach drive is through Canada
4+ litres water - there is no reliable water on the ridge
Headlamp with spare batteries - a 13+ hour day is normal
Long sleeves and gloves for brush and deadfall
Downloaded offline map and GPX of your ascent line
High-calorie food for a long day

detailed_rack: Not a rock rack route. The functional kit is a general mountaineering one: steel or aluminium crampons, a general-mountaineering ice axe, a helmet, and boots stiff enough to front-point on the middle snowfield. Parties that bring a rope carry a 30 m half or twin line, four or five slings, a couple of medium nuts and two locking carabiners — enough to sling a horn for a short lower over the 7,600 ft step. Do not expect that gear to be usable more broadly: reports from this face and the neighbouring routes are consistent that the Hozomeen chert takes protection poorly and that placements are mostly ornamental.
pro_needs: Effectively none, and that is the point. The climbing is easy enough to solo and loose enough that most parties judge a rope a liability rather than an asset above the snow. Protect yourself with snow technique and movement discipline, not hardware.
what_to_bring: Passport or NEXUS card - the drive is through Canada
Printed NPS wilderness permit for the ridge camp
Full-size spare tire for Silver-Skagit Road
4+ litres water capacity - nothing runs above the forest creeks
Bear canister if required for your zone
Full mosquito defence - reports single them out on the approach
Sunscreen and lip balm for the snowfields
Map, compass and downloaded offline track
Extra insulation - the summit is windy even in July

detailed_rack: A light alpine rack is typical: a handful of small-to-medium stoppers, one or two small cams, and several slings for horn/block anchors, plus a 60-meter rope to protect and rappel the summit block. A helmet is recommended given loose rock in the approach gullies.
pro_needs: Protection needs are modest — small stoppers and cams protect the short technical step to the top of the summit block, and slings back up horns or blocks for the rappel anchor.
rack: Several slings for horn/block rappel anchor
60m rope to protect and rappel the summit block

detailed_rack: Rope (a 75-ft/23m rope has been used for short belays/lowers on the ridge), harness, crampons, ice axe, a few snow pickets for the glacier sections, and a light rock rack for the 4th-class ridge and summit gully.
pro_needs: Snow pickets protect the Ruth and Icy Glacier crossings; the 4th-class summit ridge/gully takes slings and small gear over generally sound rock.
what_to_bring: Overnight gear if camping at Ruth Mountain or the saddle
Extra layers for a long, exposed ridge crossing
Map/GPS for the glacier and col navigation

detailed_rack: A rope and a light-to-moderate alpine rack (nuts, small-to-mid cams, slings) for the exposed low-5th-class pitches; ice axe and possibly crampons for the snowfield/small glacier depending on conditions.
pro_needs: Protection for several exposed Class 4 / low-5th-class pitches on poor rock, including the steep chimney/roof move below the summit.

detailed_rack: Single set of cams .1-3in, doubled .3-1in, a set of nuts, extra cord/slings and a few pins for tat replacement, single 60m rope; add crampons and ice axe for the Terror Glacier crossing.
pro_needs: Standard alpine rock rack; most pitches protect well with cams. Carry a little extra cord since rappel anchors are remote fixed tat (rebuilt June 2024).
what_to_bring: Crampons + ice axe for the Terror Glacier
Sturdy approach shoes for the long, steep boot path
Bear canister (loanable free at the Wilderness Information Center, Marblemount)
Light bivy/camp gear for Terror Basin

detailed_rack: Climbers should bring a double rack of nuts and cams ranging from micronuts to #4 Camalots with one #5 Camalot. Include a single set of offset cams, 5 each of beaks in various sizes, 2 lost arrows for aid placement, and 10 rivet hangers (some in #1 size for deeper rivets). Two sets of hooks are essential given the blank sections requiring creative aid placements. A quality portaledge with fly and rain shell is non-negotiable, as afternoon seepage creates waterfall conditions on pitches 5-6. The route features bolted anchors, but climbers should verify anchor condition before committing full body weight and be prepared for occasional loose bolts.
pro_needs: Protection is a mix of aid placements and bolted anchors. Lower pitches rely on crack climbing with natural protection (nuts and cams), while upper pitches require rivet placements, hooks, and beaks on blank sections. The route features some bolted anchors already in place from the first ascent, but climbers must assess anchor condition, bring spares for critical bivy sites, and be prepared for creative placements on sections lacking traditional cracks.
rack: Double rack of nuts and cams (micronuts to #4 Camalot, single #5)
Portaledge with fly and rain shell
Two 60m/70m ropes (lead line + static haul line)
what_to_bring: Helmet (mandatory for rockfall and rappel hazards)
Carabiners and lockers (large selection for rivet placements)
Slings and cord for anchor backup
Chalk bag and tape for hands
First aid kit including blister management and wound care
Headlamps with extra batteries for early starts and late climbs
Water bottles and hydration system (1-2 liters per climber per day minimum)
High-calorie food for 6-7 days of climbing (focus on high-energy, lightweight options)
Sunscreen and lip balm with SPF
Sleeping bag rated to 20 degrees F (insulation required on portaledge)

detailed_rack: No published rack exists. For Class 4 on loose greenstone with a glacier approach, carry a 60 m rope, harnesses, a light rock rack (a set of nuts, a couple of small-to-medium cams, and a generous set of slings and long runners for blocks and horns), plus tat and spare nuts for rappel anchors on the way down. Add ice axe, crampons, two snow pickets and a crevasse-rescue kit for the glacier approach the published account implies.
pro_needs: Sparse. Class 4 on Jack's rock is mostly unprotectable, and slings over blocks will be your main protection. Carry enough to build anchors for a retreat rather than expecting to protect the climbing continuously.
what_to_bring: Headlamp and spare batteries - this is a long day
Map, compass and GPS with your intended approach line loaded
2-3 L water capacity plus a filter
Tent, bag and stove for 3-4 nights

detailed_rack: A snow rack, not a rock rack. Carry a 60 m rope per rope team, harnesses, a full crevasse-rescue kit (prusiks, pulley, three or four locking carabiners), and three to four snow pickets — pickets are the workhorse here, used for the bergschrund, for running belays on the headwall and for lowering on the descent. Two ice screws are worth carrying for the years when the headwall turns out to be ice rather than neve. Most parties climb with one axe plus one technical tool each; on the winter ascent through the cliff band, teams carried one technical and one straight-shafted tool per climber plus cams, nuts, hexes and screws. Add snowshoes or skis for the approach and glacier, which most parties use.
pro_needs: Pickets for snow, screws as a backup for ice, and a rock anchor or two only if the headwall's cliff band is melted out and you must climb mixed ground. In good May conditions most parties place almost nothing and simul-climb the headwall, so protection is more about having a retreat plan than about protecting the leader.
what_to_bring: Tent, sleeping bag and stove for 2-3 nights
Shell and insulating layers - the north cirque is cold and shaded
Headlamp and spare batteries (long pre-dawn starts and a real chance of finishing in the dark)
GPS with the bushwhack line recorded on the way up - navigating the timber at night is the crux of many trips
Sunglasses and full sun protection for the glacier
2-3 L water capacity and a stove to melt snow at a glacier camp
Gaiters and gear you do not mind soaking on the bushwhack
Skis or a splitboard if you want the descent as a bonus - the glacier has been skied

detailed_rack: No published rack. For Grade II Class 4 on loose greenstone with a brushy north-side approach: a 60 m rope, harnesses, a set of nuts, a couple of small-to-medium cams, plenty of long slings and runners for blocks and horns, plus tat and spare nuts for rappel anchors. Ice axe and crampons are worth carrying for lingering north-aspect snow patches on the approach and in the ridge's gullies even in August; a picket or two if you expect a snow apron at the base.
pro_needs: Minimal and unreliable. Slings over blocks are the main protection; expect long unprotectable stretches. Carry gear primarily so you can build anchors to retreat, not to protect the climbing continuously.
what_to_bring: Shell and insulating layers for a shaded north aspect
GPS with your approach track recorded on the way up - essential for finding the line back down through the timber
2-3 L water capacity plus a filter
Tent, bag and stove for 3-4 nights

detailed_rack: Standard glacier travel kit — rope, crevasse-rescue gear, pickets, ice axe and crampons — for the steep, heavily crevassed glacier described in the 1978 FA account, plus a light rock rack for the class 4 rock near the summit ridge.
pro_needs: Snow and ice protection dominates: pickets for neve, screws where the glacier is hard, and running belays for crevasse-riddled terrain. Rock protection is limited to whatever the loose greenstone summit block offers.
what_to_bring: Snowshoes or skis for the approach in early season
Shell and insulating layers for a north-facing cirque
Bivy or tent, bag and stove for 3-4 nights
Map, compass and GPS with your intended line preloaded

detailed_rack: No published rack exists for this line. Given Grade III at 5.6 on Hozameen greenstone, a standard North Cascades alpine rack is appropriate: a single set of nuts, cams from small to about 2 inches, a generous number of slings and long runners for the blocky crest, a 60 m rope (the same rope the approach glacier requires), and enough tat and a couple of spare nuts to build rappel anchors on the way down if you reverse the ridge. Add ice axe, crampons, two snow pickets and a crevasse-rescue kit for the Jerry Glacier, which is unavoidable on the approach.
pro_needs: Expect thin and unreliable protection. The rock on Jack is loose metavolcanic greenstone, and even where the ridge offers cracks the placements need scrutiny. Long slings over blocks and horns will do much of the work; plan to run it out on easier ground and save gear for the 5.6 sections.
what_to_bring: 2-3 L water capacity per person plus a filter
Approach shoes plus mountaineering boots for the glacier
Map, compass and GPS with the cross-country line loaded
Head net and repellent for Jerry Lakes
Tent, bag and stove for 3-4 nights

detailed_rack: No published rack exists for this line. For Class 4 on loose greenstone: a 60 m rope, harnesses, a set of nuts, one or two small-to-medium cams, and plenty of long slings and runners for blocks and horns, plus tat and spare nuts for rappel anchors. Ice axe and crampons are worth carrying for snow patches on the traverse and in the ridge's gullies outside high summer. No glacier is crossed on this approach, so a full crevasse-rescue kit is not needed unless you plan to exit over Jerry Lakes.
pro_needs: Sparse and unreliable, as on every route on this peak. Slings over blocks will do most of the work; expect long unprotectable stretches and plan to move together on ground you are happy soloing.
what_to_bring: Large water capacity - the Little Jack crest is dry in late summer
Map, compass and GPS with the ridge line loaded
Sun protection for an exposed south-west facing crest
Tent, bag and stove for 2-3 nights

detailed_rack: Ice axe, a useful second tool for the steeper snow, crampons, a couple of pickets, a rope, and a helmet. No rock gear is generally needed beyond a few slings on the ridge.
pro_needs: Protection is limited to pickets in the couloir and the occasional sling on the ridge. This is a steep-snow and endurance route where conditions and timing matter more than gear.

detailed_rack: A single to double rack of cams from 0.4 to 3 inches, a set of nuts, about 10 alpine draws with doubles, two ropes for rappels, plus ice axe and crampons for the snow and ice sections.
