pro_needs: The rock pitches protect reasonably on the better stone, but much of the route is moderate, run-out, or mixed terrain where speed and judgment matter more than gear. Snow and ice sections take occasional pickets or screws.
what_to_bring: single to double rack plus nuts

detailed_rack: A small rock rack (frequently unusable in the loose/vegetated terrain), crampons, ice axe or tools, and a light rope.
pro_needs: Protection is frequently unusable through the vegetated and loose sections — much of the route should be treated as run-out; save gear for the ~700-ft crux rock band where placements are better.
what_to_bring: Bivy gear — many parties bivy near the glacier below the summit
Optional snow protection/ice screws for later-season conditions

detailed_rack: No rock rack is needed - this is an unroped Class 3 scramble. A helmet is recommended for the short rock chimney near 5,100 ft and the loose rock around it, and many parties carry an ice axe and/or microspikes for lingering snow near Melakwa Pass early in the season.
pro_needs: None required in normal dry summer conditions; not a roped-protection route.

detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard scramble by late summer. For ascents before the gully has melted out (roughly before August), bring a lightweight glacier/steep-snow kit: an ice axe and a pair of lightweight crampons suitable for 40-45° snow, plus the skills to self-arrest and downclimb steep snow. Some parties carry a short handline or a single rope with a few slings and a picket/cordelette for the summit block or any wet/icy sections, though this is not standard on the dry-season line.
pro_needs: Most parties scramble unroped; a short rope is reassuring for the class 4 crux and for less-experienced partners.
what_to_bring: Ice axe (crampons too if climbing before August)
Helmet — effectively mandatory given the loose rock
Sturdy approach shoes/boots for scree, slab, and talus
Extra food/fuel buffer — Ragged Ridge weather and route-finding can add a day
Map/compass or GPS — the gully/rib system above the 7,400 ft bench is not obvious

detailed_rack: Standard 2-pitch ice rack: a set of ice screws (including a stubby or two for thin sections), cord/webbing for V-thread rappel anchors, two ice tools per climber, and crampons. No fixed gear exists on the route.
pro_needs: Ice screws for both leading and V-thread rappel anchors; no bolts or fixed pro reported.
what_to_bring: Avalanche gear (beacon/probe/shovel) for the slide-path crossing between pitches
Approach skis or snowshoes if approaching on snow

detailed_rack: No technical rack; ice axe valuable early season for snow on the PCT traverse and summit slopes.
pro_needs: None.
what_to_bring: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful interagency pass for trailhead parking
free self-issue wilderness permit (fill out at the trailhead)
map or GPS track — the boot path is unmarked and easy to lose
extra layers — the Katwalk and summit ridge are fully exposed to wind

detailed_rack: Ice axe, crampons, climbing harness, 30m+ glacier travel rope, crevasse rescue kit (2 prusik cords or mechanical ascenders, pulley, locking carabiners), helmet, glacier glasses and sunscreen (high UV/reflectivity on open snow), trekking poles for the long approach. Group gear: detailed map/compass or GPS with route track, water filter/treatment, and standard overnight camping gear for the 2-3 day trip.
pro_needs: Glacier/snow protection where present; minimal rock pro
what_to_bring: Water filter or treatment (no potable water at high camp)
GPS with a pre-loaded route track, or detailed map and compass
Satellite communicator (InReach/spot) - no cell coverage in the wilderness interior
Rain shell - weather changes quickly even in mid-summer

detailed_rack: Not a roped rock climb for most parties. Many carry a light glacier/scramble kit (axe, microspikes or light crampons for early/late-season snow) plus a helmet for the loose summit block; parties uneasy on the exposed class 3-4 finish sometimes rig a short hand-line.
pro_needs: No fixed protection reported; natural rock/slings only if rigging a hand-line on the summit block.

detailed_rack: A glacier travel kit (rope, crevasse-rescue gear, axe, crampons) for the Pride Glacier crossing; a light rack/slings for the Class 3 rock band is optional for most parties.
pro_needs: No fixed protection reported; natural rock/slings if protecting the class 3 band, plus standard crevasse-rescue anchors on the glacier.
what_to_bring: Map/compass or GPS for Quartz Basin cliff-band navigation
Wands or a GPS track for the glacier crossing in whiteout
Overnight gear if splitting the approach over two days

detailed_rack: No technical rack is needed for this unroped scramble; carry an ice axe and microspikes/light traction for the approach gully and any residual snow patches into mid-summer, plus trekking poles for the steep, loose talus.
pro_needs: No technical protection is used on this Class 2-3 talus scramble; carry an ice axe (and know how to self-arrest) if climbing early season while snow lingers near La Bohn Gap.
what_to_bring: map/compass or GPS track for the unmaintained La Bohn Creek boot path
satellite communicator (no cell coverage beyond US 2)

detailed_rack: Single ice axe per climber (50cm+ technical or straight shaft aluminum). Crampons rated for steep ice (12-point recommended for crux sections). Climbing helmet mandatory for rockfall protection. Boot crampons compatibility essential.
pro_needs: Screws and pickets per conditions; rock pro for belays
rack: Small-medium cams (up to 2in) for rock margins of the couloir

detailed_rack: Ice axe and crampons for the ~45-degree snow, and a helmet - rockfall out of the walls is the main hazard once the sun hits. A rope and a couple of pickets only if you plan to belay, or in a lean year when the exit runs to ice; ice screws are rarely used here and are not worth carrying in a normal snow year. Avalanche kit (beacon, shovel, probe): the couloir is a terrain trap and most ascents are mid-winter to spring.
pro_needs: A couple of pickets if belaying; ice screws only in a lean year when the exit runs to ice

detailed_rack: Standard glacier-travel kit is required for the approach (rope, harness, crevasse-rescue gear, glacier axe, crampons); the class-4 summit ledges are typically soloed or protected minimally with a short rope for confidence on exposed steps.
pro_needs: Minimal fixed protection is used on the class 4 summit terrain; the technical requirement is glacier travel gear (axe, crampons, rope, crevasse rescue rack) for the approach rather than rock protection.
what_to_bring: Overnight camping gear (tent, stove, bear canister/food storage)
Sun protection for extended glacier travel

detailed_rack: Crevasse rescue kit: 60m rope (half-rope system acceptable), harnesses for party, carabiners (6+ lockers), belay/rescue anchors, ascenders. Rock protection: minimal needed (party size and conditions determine); medium-sized quickdraws (3-4) and runners sufficient for any belay anchors. Ice tools: crampons, ice axes, and helmet for all party members. Consider bringing 2-3 slings (runner length) for anchor building on rock.
pro_needs: Moderate alpine mountaineering protection needed for optional rappels; glacier travel requires standard crevasse rescue gear (harness, rope, carabiners) despite minimal crevasses on Lemah Glacier. Natural rock protection is good where needed for belayed downclimbs.
rack: 60m rope (half-rope system acceptable) for glacier travel and the short technical section
A few small cams and nuts for the exposed class 4 moves
2-3 slings for anchor building on rock
Crevasse-rescue kit: harnesses, 6+ locking carabiners, ascenders

detailed_rack: Glacier travel gear (rope, crevasse-rescue kit, ice axe, crampons) for the Lemah Glacier approach, plus a 60m rope and a rock rack of nuts and small-to-mid cams for the tower itself and its rappel descent.
pro_needs: Unknown and undocumented. Treat the protection as unsurveyed: expect to place your own on rock that is likely loose, and to leave anchors on the way down.
what_to_bring: Overnight kit for a camp at Pete Lake or the Lemah Creek PCT campsite
Insect repellent for the wet Lemah meadows
USGS Chikamin Peak quad plus a GPS track for the cross-country section
Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit
Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass for the car

detailed_rack: No rope typically carried; ice axe and crampons are the main technical items and are used minimally outside of early-season snow.
pro_needs: None beyond an ice axe for occasional steep snow; this is a cross-country/scrambling traverse, not a technical roped climb.
what_to_bring: Wilderness permits for Upper Lena Lake and Lake of the Angels camps
Navigation aids for foggy, way-trail sections

detailed_rack: No rock gear. Summer: trekking poles and boots with decent tread are the whole kit. Winter: skis with skins or snowshoes, plus the standard avalanche kit — transceiver, probe and shovel, worn and practised with, not carried as decoration. An ice axe is worth having in spring or after a freeze-thaw cycle for the firm slopes below the saddle; ski crampons help on the road and lower slopes when the track is icy in the morning.
pro_needs: None. There is no protectable rock climbing on this route and no fixed anchors anywhere on the mountain.
what_to_bring: Offline topo maps and a downloaded GPX track
NWAC Stevens Pass avalanche forecast checked the morning of the trip
2 litres of water plus a filter (Lichtenwasser Lake in summer)
Insect repellent in July and August
Insulation and shell adequate for a windy summit ridge
Goggles and warm gloves in winter
Northwest Forest Pass for the dashboard

detailed_rack: Two 60-meter dynamic ropes are standard. Belay anchors use a combination of ice screws (4-6 total; typically #2-#3 Grivel or Black Diamond), natural rock slings, and pickets placed in snow. Most rappel anchors are natural horns slung with webbing or dynamic sling material. Crampons should have rigid front points suitable for 70-80 degree ice. Two ice axes: one for climbing, one for safety. Approximately 6-8 pickets for snow anchors.
pro_needs: Pickets and a light rack; much of the rock is too loose to protect well
rack: Small rack: 4 small cams + small nut set

detailed_rack: No technical rock gear is needed. An ice axe is worthwhile early in the season for snow on the upper slopes, and trekking poles help on the talus.
pro_needs: There is no protectable climbing; movement is unroped scrambling. The challenge is minimal beyond basic route-finding and staying back from the south edge.

detailed_rack: Light alpine kit rather than a rock rack. One 60 m rope is enough for the documented rappels: a winter party carried two 60 m ropes, used them together for one rappel from near the top, and found a single rope would have done at the col. Bring a picket or two for snow anchors, a few nuts and slings for rock anchors on the mixed ground near the summit, and plenty of cord or webbing plus rap rings; there are no reliable fixed anchors, so plan to leave gear. A mountaineering axe each is the usual tool, and the winter ascent was made on single axes.
pro_needs: Protection is thin and improvised. The south-side gully is snow and rock, climbed unroped in good conditions, with a bit of mixed ground near the summit where the dunite offers occasional horns, blocks and small nut placements; it is coarse and generally solid but is not a splitter-crack medium. Expect to move unroped or run it out on moderate snow and save your gear for anchors. Because you will rappel, budget cord and rings for two stations you may have to build from scratch.
what_to_bring: Snowshoes or approach skis for the lower Green Creek basin
Headlamp plus spare batteries (the documented exit was after dark)
Sturdy boots and dry socks for the unbridged Middle Fork Nooksack log crossing
GPS or phone with the track preloaded offline
Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass for the trailhead
Small first aid and repair kit
Bike, if FR 38 is gated at Wallace Creek

detailed_rack: Typical glacier rope-team kit: one rope (~30m class) per 2-3 person team, harness, 2-3 snow pickets, crevasse-rescue kit (prusiks or mechanical ascenders, pulley, spare carabiners), ice axe, crampons; helmet is essential for the entire glacier-to-summit sequence, not just the scramble.
pro_needs: None on the scramble; glacier protection as conditions dictate.
what_to_bring: climbing registration and wilderness permit paperwork

detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the class 3 scramble itself. The real gear need is standard summer glacier-travel kit for the approach: a rope per team, harness, crevasse-rescue hardware (prusik cords, pulley/ascender), ice axe, and crampons for crossing the Le Conte, South Cascade, and other glaciers between Cascade Pass and Lizard Col.
pro_needs: Protection needs are almost entirely about the glacier approach rather than the summit scramble: a rope for each glacier-travel team, a full crevasse-rescue kit, and a helmet for rockfall/icefall exposure along the traverse.

detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard scramble; carry an ice axe and crampons whenever snow lingers on the approach slopes, ledges, or ridge crest (common into midsummer and again in early fall).
pro_needs: No rock protection is needed for the scrambling, which is climbed unroped. A glacier rope with crevasse-rescue gear is needed for the upper Richardson Glacier crossing, and a few slings for a natural rappel anchor at the short step below the East Ridge; parties uneasy on the exposed Class 3+ ground near the summit may want a light rack as well.
what_to_bring: Printed map and/or GPS track — there is no cell coverage in this drainage
Bivy/overnight buffer gear given documented 15-18+ hour car-to-car days

detailed_rack: A light alpine rack: runners and a few pieces of trad gear (small-to-medium) for the class 4-5 slab pitches, plus glacier travel gear (crampons, axe, and pickets) for the hanging glacier and bergschrund below.
pro_needs: Protection for the rock is simply runners and a few pieces of gear, supplemented by standard glacier-travel protection for the snow/ice approach.
rack: Light rack: a few cams and nuts (runners and a few pieces of gear)
A few snow pickets or flukes for the glacier crux
Single rope for rappelling/downclimbing off the summit block
Crampons and ice axe for the glacier crossing
what_to_bring: Bug head-net — Luna Cirque's flies are notorious in July
Satellite communicator (inReach/Zoleo); no cell coverage in the Pickets
Bear canister or Ursack for food storage

detailed_rack: Ice axe and crampons essential for snow/ice. Optional: 50-60m rope for belayed crux; many solo. Helmet essential. Minimal rock gear.
pro_needs: Varies by experience. Single 50m rope with harness/slings for crux. Self-rescue knowledge essential.

detailed_rack: Small alpine rack (6-7 pieces), 30 m rope, 3 runners with carabiners, slings for trees, rappel device; published descriptions list helmet as optional, though most parties wear one given the loose rock.
pro_needs: Light trad rack for the short Class 4/5.0 sections and tree/gear anchors for the rappel; the route is short enough that protection needs are minimal compared to the routefinding and loose-rock hazard.

detailed_rack: Glacier travel kit (axe, crampons, rope, crevasse rescue gear) for the Yawning Glacier and couloir; rock rack for the class 4 face is minimal (natural gear/slings), helmet essential.
pro_needs: Standard glacier travel protection (pickets/screws as conditions dictate) plus a light rack for optional protection on the class 4 face.
what_to_bring: Overnight camping gear for Pelton Basin

detailed_rack: This is a snow route, so the rack is snow and glacier hardware rather than rock gear. Carry an ice axe and, for the 45-50 degree upper section, a second tool or a technical axe. Two or three pickets cover belays and running protection on the steepest ground; one or two ice screws are worth having for the firm crust reported near the top and for a hard bergschrund lip on the glacier. A 40-50 m rope handles both roped glacier travel and any belayed pitches in the couloir. Full avalanche kit — transceiver, shovel, probe — is mandatory in the season this route is in condition. If you expect the lean-year rock finish, add a small selection of nuts and long slings for block anchors on the broken gneiss.
pro_needs: On snow, protection is pickets and, where the crust is hard, screws — most parties solo the lower and middle couloir and belay or run out pickets on the top 100-200 ft where the angle reaches 50 degrees. The Yawning Glacier below requires roped travel and a functioning crevasse-rescue system. In a lean year the finish is rock rather than snow, and then the route needs a handful of nuts and long slings for slung-block belays on broken gneiss, with the caveat that there are no fixed anchors anywhere on this peak.
what_to_bring: Wilderness permit for Pelton Basin Camp (designated site, limited capacity)
Satellite messenger — no cell coverage on this side of the pass
Full avalanche kit: transceiver, shovel, probe
Approved food storage; Pelton Basin has bear boxes
Water filter or treatment — the Pelton Basin creek is the source
Headlamp with spare batteries for a pre-dawn start
Warm layers and gloves: the couloir is shaded and cold until the sun arrives, and then you should already be leaving
Offline topo showing both the Yawning Glacier descent and the South Ridge walk-off

detailed_rack: Light rock rack/slings for the steep rock and chimney section; helmet recommended.
pro_needs: Protection is sparse and improvised. The steep rock below the chimney is the section where a rope is most likely to come out, but the broken gneiss takes cams poorly and you will get more from slinging features than from placing gear. Most competent parties move together or solo the Class 4, using the rope only for a nervous partner or for a retreat. The chimney is described as easy and generally needs nothing. The genuinely protectable moments on the day are on the Cache Glacier during the approach and exit.

detailed_rack: Minimal — an unroped heather/rock scramble; helmet recommended for loose rock.
pro_needs: Effectively none — this is a protection-free route by design. The gullies are heather, dirt and broken gneiss; there is nothing to place and nothing fixed. Parties that want security should bring a short rope for hand-lines and rely on slung heather clumps and blocks, understanding that these are psychological rather than real anchors. The one place a rope earns its weight is the Cache Glacier on the approach and exit, where roped travel and a crevasse-rescue system are appropriate.

detailed_rack: A standard alpine rock rack (small-to-medium cams/nuts) for the 5.6 pitch, plus glacier travel gear (axe, crampons) for the pocket glacier and schrund crossing.
pro_needs: Natural/gear protection on the 5.6 open-book pitch; the schrund crossing may require a picket or ice screw depending on conditions.

detailed_rack: A single 30-60m rope with a light rack — a handful of small-to-mid cams/nuts and a few slings — is enough to protect the roped Class 3-4 sections and the exposed Class 4 crux gully below the summit. Many strong scrambling parties climb the route unroped in dry conditions; a helmet is recommended given the loose rock.
pro_needs: Most parties travel unroped; a rope and a few slings/a picket cover the single optional rappel near the summit for those who don't want to downclimb the Class 4 step.
rack: Light rack: a few small-to-mid cams and nuts
A few slings for natural anchors (horns, chockstones, trees)
30-60m rope for the crux gully / exposed step near the summit
what_to_bring: Ice axe (early-season snow near Holden Pass)
Trekking poles for the scree/gully sections

detailed_rack: No technical rock gear is needed for the standard scramble. An ice axe is worth carrying early in the season for snow on shaded slopes, and trekking poles help on the long talus approach and ascent.
pro_needs: There is no protectable climbing on the easiest line; movement is unroped scrambling. The demands are navigation and stamina across a broad mountain rather than any gear.

detailed_rack: A medium alpine rock rack — small-to-mid cams and a set of nuts — plus 8-10 shoulder-length runners for the long, wandering pitches, a helmet, and a single ice axe for the shared glacier and snow approach. Matches the published route description.
pro_needs: Standard alpine rock protection to about 2-3 inches with 8-10 runners to manage rope drag on the long, wandering pitches. The crux final pitch (5.8- PG13) protects only moderately well. Helmet and a single ice axe for the shared glacier approach.
rack: 1 snow picket + ice axe for approach
what_to_bring: bivy/camping gear for a 2-3 day trip
approach shoes/boots suited to brush and slab
extra layers for exposed ridge climbing

detailed_rack: A technical rack is optional rather than mandatory. Most parties carry an ice axe and crampons for the Terror Glacier crossing and the snow/ice gully to the col, plus a helmet for loose rock above. Some parties bring a light rope and a small rack of cams/nuts to protect the short exposed class 3-4 step below the summit block, but many climb the entire route unroped.
pro_needs: Minimal protection needed overall — a light rack of a few slings/small cams or nuts covers the short, exposed class 3-4 step near the summit; the rope is mostly for security and an optional short rappel rather than sustained pitched climbing.
what_to_bring: 30m rope and a light rack for the summit step
bear canister (recommended for Terror Basin camp)
bivy/camping gear for a 2-3 day trip
water treatment (no reliable water source between the top of the hillclimb and Terror Basin)
sturdy mountaineering boots suited to scrambling and snow travel
navigation (map/GPS/compass) for the unmarked, unmaintained approach trail
bear canister if required for the camping zone

detailed_rack: A light rack suffices: ice axe and crampons for the steep snow to the North Col, a 60m rope, a helmet, and a handful of small-to-medium stoppers and slings for the ~30 ft bolted 5.6 chimney. A single rappel off the bolted anchor descends the chimney.
pro_needs: A few small-to-medium cams and/or slings for the ~30-75 ft chimney (reported as three roped moves: 5.6, 5.2, 5.6); a 60m rope covers the technical section and its rappel. Fixed bolts have been reported in recent years but should not be solely relied upon.
rack: 60m rope for the roped chimney section and its rappel (three moves: 5.6, 5.2, 5.6)
A few small cams/nuts, optional, as backup to reported (unconfirmed) bolts
2-3 slings for a gully belay/rappel anchor

detailed_rack: No technical rack; ice axe useful early season for snow in the basin.
pro_needs: None.
what_to_bring: Green Trails Mountain Loop Highway No. 111SX map
Northwest Forest Pass or day-use fee

detailed_rack: Per person: two technical ice tools, crampons, helmet, harness. Per team: 30–60 m rope, 6–8 ice screws, 3–4 pickets, V-thread tool, crevasse-rescue and rappel gear.
pro_needs: Glacier ice protection — ice screws for the steep steps and pickets for snow, plus full crevasse-rescue capability. No rock pro.

detailed_rack: Per person: ice axe (second tool useful in firm conditions), crampons, helmet, harness. Per team: 30–40 m rope, 2–4 pickets, crevasse-rescue kit for the summit ice cap.
pro_needs: Snow protection (pickets) for the steeper upper ridge plus glacier-travel gear for the summit ice cap; generally no rock pro.

detailed_rack: A snow picket, at least one ice screw, a few thin pitons, and two ice tools.
pro_needs: Minimal rack: picket(s) and a screw or two for the steepest 50° sections.

detailed_rack: Ice axe and crampons or microspikes depending on snow coverage; helmet recommended for loose rock near Pikers Peak.
pro_needs: No technical protection is used on the standard line; ice axe and crampons only — rope and glacier gear are not needed.
what_to_bring: Sun protection (glacier glasses, sunscreen, lip balm)
Extra water/filter (scarce above Lunch Counter early season)
Layered clothing for wind and whiteout

detailed_rack: No rock rack needed beyond glacier gear — ice axe, crampons, and 2-3 pickets are the core kit; a screw or two can be useful for the steepened Flypaper finger or any exposed bergschrund lip in late season.
pro_needs: Primarily snow and glacier protection; little to no rock protection on the brief summit scramble.
what_to_bring: bear canister (free loaners available from the Wilderness Information Center in Port Angeles)
gaiters for postholing on the snow finger and glacier
mountain bike (optional, to speed the road-walk sections)

detailed_rack: 30m glacier rope (1 per team), 1 picket per person for belays, full crevasse-rescue kit (4-6 pickets, 1 ice screw, slings, carabiners, ascenders), crampons, ice axe, helmet, harness
pro_needs: Glacier rope team dynamics, crevasse rescue setup, route-finding skills for mid-route navigation

detailed_rack: Glacier rope team: 30–40 m rope, 2–4 pickets, crevasse-rescue kit (prusiks, pulleys), 1–2 ice screws late season. Per person: ice axe, crampons, helmet, harness, locking biners.
pro_needs: Glacier protection only — pickets for the Roman Wall and running belays through crevasse zones.

detailed_rack: Typically 3-5 ice screws and 2-4 snow pickets, two ice tools per person, glacier/crevasse-rescue kit, and a rope for belayed pitches; a light rock rack is not needed.
pro_needs: Ice screws and pickets for the steep headwall

detailed_rack: Glacier rope team: 30–40 m rope, 2–4 pickets, crevasse-rescue kit, 1–2 screws late season. Per person: ice axe, crampons, helmet, harness, locking biners.
pro_needs: Glacier protection only — pickets for the Roman Wall and crevasse zones.

detailed_rack: 5-7 ice screws, a handful of pickets, two ice tools per person, rope and crevasse-rescue kit for the glacier approach, plus gear for 2-6 belayed ice pitches at the crux cliff.
pro_needs: Ice screws for the headwall ice pitches, pickets for snow, full crevasse-rescue capability. No rock pro.

detailed_rack: Glacier rope, harness, crevasse-rescue kit, ice axe, crampons, pickets — basic glacier-travel gear, similar to Easton Glacier.
pro_needs: Pickets for crevasse-rescue anchoring; no fixed protection.
what_to_bring: Early-season timing to avoid the late-season bergschrund

detailed_rack: No rack is needed. Bring a helmet for the loose summit gully, and an ice axe while early-season snow lingers on the upper mountain.
pro_needs: No fixed protection exists on the route. It is a Class 3 scramble with a few short, exposed steps near the summit block, normally climbed unroped.

detailed_rack: Class 2-3 scrambling terrain; most parties carry no technical rock rack. An ice axe (and possibly crampons) is recommended in early season for the snow finger/gully below the roughly 7,650 ft saddle.
pro_needs: Not a technical rock route in the sustained-protection sense; the objective hazards are steep snow and loose/exposed rock rather than sustained climbing, so protection needs are minimal — ice axe and crampons for the snow finger and gully, helmet for rockfall, with a short rope/light rack as optional insurance on the steepest slabby moves.

detailed_rack: Not a roped climb for the standard Class 3 line in normal summer conditions. A helmet is explicitly recommended due to loose rock in the cliff-band scramble. For early-season (May-June) attempts when snow lingers in the approach gullies and on the cliff bands, carry an ice axe and consider crampons/microspikes; some parties doing the full multi-peak Sawtooth Slam traverse have carried full ice axe and crampons for adjoining terrain.
pro_needs: Unroped class 2-3 scramble; no technical gear normally required.

detailed_rack: A double rack to 3 inches is what the first-ascent party carried and what they recommended. They also brought a #4 and used it twice but noted it was not really necessary for the line they chose, and they placed very little small gear — so weight the rack toward hands, fists and off-hands rather than micro-cams and small nuts. Doubles of cams from about 0.5 to #3 covers the fist bulge on pitch 2, the S-crack on pitch 3, and the double fist-and-wider cracks above the crux, where the FA leader ran out of gear and had to traverse off onto face holds to find a stance. A single set of nuts is worth having for the corner and dihedral on pitch 2. A single 60 m rope suffices — the longest pitch is 35 m — and doubles as a rappel line for retreat, though you will leave gear if you use it. Bring a nut tool, and bring a wire brush or two: the FA party's single strongest gear note was that cleaning lichen, sand and brittle flakes by hand and boot was what made the climbing slow, and that brushes would have been worth the weight.
pro_needs: Protection is all natural on a crack line with no fixed gear, no bolts and no fixed anchors reported. Placements are good where the cracks are clean but frequently need excavating first, so factor cleaning time into every placement. The wide double cracks above the pitch-3 crux are the section most likely to leave you short — a party that has spent its #2s and #3s low will be running it out there. Belays are on gear at natural stances: an alcove at the base of the fist bulge, a small ledge beside a triangular perched block, and a stance next to a small tower on the summit ridge. Be deliberate about anchor blocks on a lichenous, lightly travelled face; test everything.
what_to_bring: Wire brush (or two) for cleaning cracks — the FA party's top recommendation
Ice axe if any snow lingers on the descent slopes
Overnight kit for camping at Upper Eagle Lake
Water filter or treatment (Upper Eagle Lake is the last water)
2-3 L water capacity for the climb itself
Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass, or Digital Day Pass for the trailhead
Map and compass or GPS with the Eagle Lakes trail loaded
Binoculars for scoping the line from the lakeshore
Sun protection and a warm layer — the face goes into shade by afternoon
Insect repellent (meadows on the approach can be badly mosquito-ridden in early summer)
Bear-resistant food storage or a hang line for camp

detailed_rack: Standard alpine rock rack for moderate 5.9 granite cracks (small-to-mid cams and nuts) plus glacier travel gear (rope, harness, crevasse-rescue kit, axe, crampons) for the approach crossing.
pro_needs: Protection needed for sustained 5.8-5.9 cracks/corners on the headwall pitches gaining the ridge crest; less protection needed on the easier crest climbing above, which is more scrambling in character.
what_to_bring: Glacier travel/crevasse rescue gear for the basin crossing
Light bivy gear if splitting the route over 2 days
Approach shoes for the brushy Blum Creek approach

detailed_rack: Not a technical rock route for most parties — no fixed rack is standard. An ice axe is required for the snow gully/bowl below the south ridge in most conditions; crampons are recommended in early season or firm snow. A handful of parties carry a short rope and a few slings/light rack for the class 3-4 notch/bypass or the exposed east-face terrain some climbers inadvertently encounter.
pro_needs: Minimal fixed protection is typical; the route is graded as a scramble. Parties uncomfortable with exposed, unroped class 3-4 rock near the summit ridge should carry a rope and a small rack (a few slings, cams to ~2in) for a short belayed section.
what_to_bring: Bear canister (mandatory for overnight camping — no reliable trees for a hang)
Water treatment (reliable water at Blum Creek and the Blum Lakes; none higher on the mountain)
A GPS track or detailed trip-report notes — the approach path is unmarked and frequently confused with game trails
2-3 days of food if not attempting a very fast single-push

detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard class 4 line. Carry a basic glacier-travel kit — ice axe, crampons, and a rope with minimal crevasse-rescue hardware (pickets and/or a couple of screws depending on conditions) — for the glacier remnants on the north/east flanks, plus a helmet for the loose class 4 scrambling near the summit.
pro_needs: Glacier-travel protection (pickets, occasional screws) is the main consideration rather than rock protection; the class 4 rock is typically climbed unroped by parties comfortable with sustained exposed scrambling.

detailed_rack: No technical rock gear for the standard scramble; ice axe early season
pro_needs: None for the standard line
what_to_bring: Reserved Wilderness Camping Permit and a bear canister
Ice axe if climbing before late July or when snow lingers on north-facing terrain
Topo map/GPS for off-trail navigation above Cameron Basin
Satellite communicator — no reliable cell coverage on the approach or peak

detailed_rack: A lightweight alpine rack for scrambling: ice axe, crampons, helmet, rope (30–50m rope optional for group safety on Catwalk), and self-rescue equipment. Harness and sling recommended if roping. For water-crossing sections, consider trekking poles for stream fords.
pro_needs: Grade Class 2–3 scrambling protection: helmet mandatory for rockfall hazard, ice axe essential for early-season snow and self-arrest, crampons for frozen surfaces June–July. Rope carries psychological security on the Catwalk but is not strictly required for individuals with solid scrambling skills and comfort with exposure; recommended for groups.
rack: 30-50m rope (optional, group safety on the exposed Catwalk)
Harness and sling if roping up
what_to_bring: Layers (high-altitude, wet Pacific weather is common)
High-calorie food and electrolyte drink mix
First aid kit with blister treatment

detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard West Route scramble. Carry an ice axe and crampons for the snow ramp/gully sections below the summit pyramid, especially in early-mid season. A helmet is recommended given loose, moss-covered rock. Trekking poles help on the long brushy/heather approach. Parties attempting the harder North Ridge alternate (a distinct, separate line, not this route) should bring a light rack of cams and nuts for low-5th-class rock.
pro_needs: Standard scramble protection only: ice axe and crampons for the snow sections, no fixed rock protection required on the normal west-ridge/west-face line.
rack: Optional hand line/short rope (exposed Class 3 step near the summit)
what_to_bring: extra food/water for a long day

detailed_rack: One rope (30m+) for the team, 2-3 slings/cordage plus a couple of locking carabiners for the rappel/belay anchor, crampons, a mountaineering ice axe, harness, rappel/belay device, and a helmet.
pro_needs: A single rope (glacier travel plus the short rappel) and a handful of slings/cordage for a hasty rock anchor are sufficient -- this is not a crack- or bolt-protected pitch climb, just a short technical step needing a solid improvised anchor.
what_to_bring: rope, harness, crampons, ice axe, helmet
2-3 slings/cordage + locking carabiners for a rappel/belay anchor
headlamp with spare batteries (parties have been caught out after dark on the descent)
map/compass or GPS -- travel above Martins Park is off-trail
water treatment and bug protection for the brushy krummholz sections

detailed_rack: No cam or nut rack is needed on the standard scramble, but carry a 30 m rope and a few slings: they rig a hip belay or handline on the exposed downclimb and a natural anchor for the ~60 ft rappel off the summit block. Ice axe early season, into mid-July.
pro_needs: Minimal fixed protection is used -- this is a scramble, not a technical rock climb. Carry a 30 m rope and a few slings to rig a hip belay/handline on the exposed downclimb and a natural rappel anchor off the summit block; a cam/nut rack is typically not needed.
what_to_bring: water treatment (no reliable water at Surprise Col or on route)
30 m rope plus slings for the rappel
sun protection for the long, exposed talus/scree slopes
map/compass or GPS for the off-trail navigation through Surprise Basin

detailed_rack: No technical rock gear for the standard scramble; ice axe early season
pro_needs: None for the standard line
what_to_bring: extra food for the long approach

detailed_rack: Similar to the standard route: light rack and rope for the traverse, ice axe and crampons for the chute in early season.
pro_needs: Minimal; used mainly to protect the shared crux traverse near the top.
what_to_bring: Bear canister for Lake Constance camp
Map/compass or GPS — Avalanche Canyon is confusing terrain

detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the SW Flank scramble itself. An ice axe (and often traction) is standard for the steep snow sections of the approach ridge. Parties planning the alternative NE Ridge descent (as part of a larger traverse) commonly carry a light rope and a small rack/slings for the short 4th/5th-class downclimbing and occasional rappel.
pro_needs: Minimal rock gear — a few slings and small cams/nuts are enough for the occasional short rappel anchor or belayed step; this is a scrambling route, not a pitched rock climb.
what_to_bring: a few slings and small cams/nuts for rappel anchors
bear canister/food storage per current NPS regulations

detailed_rack: Standard glacier-travel kit for a small rope team: ice axe, crampons, climbing harness, a glacier rope (30m class is typical for 2-3 people), 2-3 locking carabiners and slings, prusiks or mechanical ascenders for crevasse rescue, and a picket or two if the glacier is still snow-covered. Helmet for the loose rock band below the glacier, plus trekking poles for the approach.
pro_needs: Minimal; glacier protection only.
what_to_bring: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit (fill out at trailhead)
Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass for the vehicle
Water treatment — Peggy's Pond is the main reliable water source in the upper basin
Sun protection (glacier travel: sunglasses/glacier goggles, sunscreen)
Satellite communicator — cell coverage is unreliable to absent in the basin

detailed_rack: Standard glacier travel kit: rope, harness, and crevasse-rescue hardware (pickets, prusiks/pulleys); no rock rack is typically needed.
pro_needs: Glacier travel protection only (snow pickets/screws as conditions dictate); no fixed rock protection is recorded for this route.
what_to_bring: Map/GPS for the long multi-lake approach (Marmot/Jade Lakes, Dip Top Gap)
Overnight backpacking gear — the approach is long enough that most parties camp
Water treatment for camps at Marmot/Jade Lakes or Pea Soup Lake

detailed_rack: Helmet is absolutely mandatory and non-negotiable. Glacier crossing requires ice axe and crampons. Bring 2-3 ice screws or snow pickets for emergency anchor points. Mountaineering backpack (50-60L) for multi-day Alpine camp. Climbing boots with aggressive tread or rock shoes for secure footwork on loose terrain. Trekking poles useful for approach but abandoned at camp for summit push. Most climbers bring lightweight rope (30-50m) for emergency situations though standard route does not require roped climbing.
pro_needs: Largely an unroped scramble; parties may want a rope and minimal gear for protecting or belaying short exposed steps depending on conditions and comfort.
rack: 2-3 ice screws or snow pickets (emergency anchor points, glacier crossing)
30-50m rope (optional, emergency use — standard route does not require roped climbing)

detailed_rack: Standard alpine rack: quickdraws, slings, stoppers, hexes, small to medium cams. Doubled slings for rappel anchors. Glacier gear: crampons, ice axe, 60-meter rope.
pro_needs: Standard trad rack for Class 4-5 rock climbing with doubled slings for rappel anchors. Glacier gear: crampons, ice axe, rope (60m recommended).
rack: Extra slings/cord for rappel anchors (weathered fixed tat on the summit tower)

detailed_rack: A rock rack sufficient for sustained 5.6 and a 5.9 crux pitch (small to mid-size cams and nuts), a 70m rope, plus extra slings/cord for building rappel anchors at the intermediate notches; snow/glacier travel gear (axe, possibly crampons) for the summit snow-ridge finish.
pro_needs: Gear is needed most for the sustained lower corner (5.6) and the crux 70m ramp pitch (5.9) through the deep cleft; natural anchors (horns, gear placements) back up the several short rappels over intermediate notches.
what_to_bring: brush-tolerant clothing for the Goodell Creek approach
extra rope/cord given the multiple short rappels over buttress notches

detailed_rack: Beyond a standard scrambling kit (ice axe, crampons, helmet), many parties carry a short rope (30-60m) with a light rack of slings and a few small pieces of protection for the brief class 4-5 exposed moves near the summit block; a picket or two is useful for firm snow on the glacier/snowfield traverse below the ridge, especially early season.
pro_needs: Mostly natural/scrambling protection; a small rack of slings and a few small cams or nuts cover the short exposed class 4-5 section near the top. Snow pickets are more useful than rock gear for most parties, for the glacier/snowfield crossing below the ridge.
rack: 30-60m rope (optional, for the exposed Class 4-5 summit moves)
A few small cams or nuts
1-2 snow pickets (glacier/snowfield traverse below the ridge)

detailed_rack: No technical rock or ice gear is needed for the South Slopes line itself. Parties commonly carry a lightweight glacier/crevasse-rescue kit (thin rope, tibloc/microtraxion, pulley, slings, a picket or two) for other glacier crossings elsewhere on the Bailey Range Traverse, plus an ice axe and simple strap-on aluminum crampons for lingering snow patches; mountaineering boots and ice screws are generally reported as unnecessary.

No technical rack is needed for the standard Class 2-3 scramble line; bring an ice axe for early-season snow on the approach and upper slopes, and a helmet is a reasonable precaution given the loose, shattered rock.
pro_needs: No technical rock protection required on the standard line; an ice axe is useful for early-season snow in the approach basins.

detailed_rack: A very small alpine rack is all this route needs. Take a handful of nuts and a set of small-to-medium cams; the 20-ft step protects well on good medium-sized cams, and a single medium chock or cam builds the rappel anchor. One 50 m or 60 m single rope (some parties use two 25 m ropes instead) covers the step and lets you rappel anything else on the 4th and low-5th ground. A half-dozen shoulder-length runners and a couple of locking carabiners are plenty. Steel crampons and an ice axe are mandatory for the approach heather, the traverse and the upper glacier, and a picket or two or a snow fluke is worth carrying for the snow you will cross.
pro_needs: A rack sufficient to protect one short 5.4 vertical step (~20 ft); otherwise the ridge is described as Class 3-4 scrambling.
what_to_bring: GPS with a downloaded track plus map and compass
satellite messenger or PLB with two-way messaging
printed photo beta of the east ridge and Point 7,850
sun hat, glacier glasses and heavy sunscreen
gaiters, leather gloves and safety glasses for the Access Creek bushwhack
water bladders (running water is scarce high on the ridge)
bear canister if required for your permitted zone
trekking poles for the heather traverse
extra food for a forced bivouac

detailed_rack: A full set of nuts and an alpine rack of cams to ~3 in with doubles in the common mid sizes, plus a few knifeblade or lost-arrow pitons to supplement anchors. Carry 12+ shoulder and double-length runners and significant extra cordage and webbing for building rappel anchors: there is no fixed gear on the route, the dozen-odd rappels off the gendarmes all come off natural blocks, horns and old tat, and the anchor material you carry is what you get down on - there is no walk-off on either flank. Double or twin 60 m ropes, or a tag line, for the long gendarme rappels. Crampons and ice axe for the glacier approach and descent.
pro_needs: Expert-level rock climbing and alpine skills required. Technical rock pitches (5.9–5.10) demand confidence in leading at grade and onsight climbing ability. Rappelling proficiency is essential (12+ rappels, some diagonal or awkward). Route finding and navigation in complex terrain are non-negotiable. Self-rescue capability strongly recommended given extreme remoteness. This is a committing alpine route with limited bailout; turnaround judgment and risk assessment must be excellent.
rack: Alpine rack of nuts/cams to ~3in, doubles in common mid sizes
A few knifeblade/lost arrow pitons (optional, supplementing rap anchors)
12+ shoulder/double-length runners plus extra cordage/webbing for rappel anchors
Tag line or twin ropes for the numerous gendarme rappels
what_to_bring: Bivy gear and stove for a multi-day ascent
Extra food/fuel buffer for weather delays

detailed_rack: A standard alpine trad rack plus snow gear. In short: a trad rack and a picket or two. In practice: a set of nuts, cams from small to about 2-3 inches, a few pitons are worth considering given the reported difficulty of finding solid placements, plenty of runners for wandering pitches, double ropes or a single 60 m plus a tag line for retreat, one or two pickets, and steel crampons and an ice axe (a second tool is worth having for the steeper snow). Rock shoes are worth carrying for the 5.9 crux - the route involves repeated snow-to-rock transitions, so a light pair pays for itself.
pro_needs: Protection is the weak point of this route. Climbers report that route-finding is tricky and the protection is not always where you want it, so expect long runouts on Class 4 and low-5th ground and plan for a rack that lets you build belays quickly in imperfect rock. Snow protection matters as much as rock - a picket or two for the couloir and for the summit arete.
what_to_bring: satellite messenger or PLB with two-way messaging
GPS with a downloaded track, plus map and compass
bivy sack and light sleeping kit for a forced bivouac on the route
stove and extra fuel plus a weather-day's food
gaiters, gloves and eye protection for the Access Creek bushwhack
bear canister if required for your zone
spare warm layers and a shell - this is a north face

detailed_rack: A light rack (a few cams/nuts) for protecting low-5th-class steps and any short raps off the towers; a single 50-60m rope, not doubles; crampons plus an ice axe (or two tools in early season) for the East Mount Fury Glacier and residual snow fingers; 2-3 pickets or ice screws for glacier travel.
pro_needs: Protection needs are moderate for the Class 5 pitches; the rock is loose and takes gear poorly, so expect to build anchors from natural horns and slung blocks. Pitons are primarily useful for backup anchors on sketchy sections, though modern climbers typically use cams and nuts. The low angle and moderate protection requirements mean self-rescue capability is more critical than full pro redundancy; if ground-up climbing is necessary, climbers must have experience with trad anchors in granite.

detailed_rack: No ropes or technical climbing gear required for the standard scramble. A climbing helmet is essential for loose rock protection. Microspikes or crampons may be necessary March through May depending on snow conditions; check avalanche forecasts and current condition reports.
pro_needs: Route-finding experience essential; faint boot trail in lower forest and terrain exposure above tree line. The route lacks marked waypoints. Topographic map and compass recommended. GPS and knowledge of scrambling terrain assessment are highly valuable for safe navigation.
what_to_bring: map & compass or GPS (extensive off-trail navigation above Methow Pass or on the Swamp Creek ridge)
layers and a rain shell (afternoon storms)
sun protection for extended above-treeline travel

detailed_rack: Ice axe and crampons for the remnant ice/snow patches; roped glacier travel is no longer typically needed now that Hinman Glacier has stopped flowing, though conditions (and thus gear needs) can vary year to year -- check recent trip reports.
pro_needs: Minimal; snow/glacier protection.

detailed_rack: No technical rack is used on the standard class 2 route — it is unroped scrambling on talus, heather, and a short rocky ridge. Some parties carry an ice axe (and occasionally microspikes) for lingering snow patches on north aspects in June/early July.
pro_needs: No technical pro; an ice axe is useful for early-season snow on the approach slopes.

detailed_rack: No technical rack is needed for the standard south-slope scramble in summer conditions — it is a talus/gully scramble up to loose class 3. An ice axe (and crampons) are commonly carried into early summer for the saddle and upper slope snow, and some parties wear a helmet through the loose rock-band gullies.
pro_needs: No technical protection is used — this is an unroped Class 2/2+ scramble with no roped pitches.
what_to_bring: extra water (unreliable sources above Crescent Lake)

detailed_rack: A light alpine rock rack (small-to-medium cams and stoppers) suits the class-5.5/5.6 pitches; a helmet is essential given the loose rock.
pro_needs: Protection on the lower pitches is on solid, exposed rock; higher and in the brushier sections, rock quality degrades and pro can be sparser.
what_to_bring: Headlamp given the long round-trip time

detailed_rack: No technical rack is needed - the standard South Slope/South Face line is an unroped Class 2-3 scramble over talus, scree, and rocky ribs. An ice axe (and possibly light traction) is worth carrying into early summer for lingering snow on the approach and summit slopes.
pro_needs: No protection is needed for this scramble route. Belay equipment is not required. Traction and stability are the primary concerns.
what_to_bring: Multi-day backpacking gear (tent, sleeping bag, stove)
Sun protection for exposed talus and ridges
Extra layers for fast-changing alpine weather
Satellite communicator (inReach or similar) given remoteness
Free self-issue wilderness permit (from trailhead register)

detailed_rack: Not a roped climb for most parties, but a light kit is prudent: helmet for the loose ridge/summit block, and some parties carry a rope with a few slings/small cams or a harness for the most exposed 3rd/4th-class moves (especially if also tagging the nearby Southwest Lincoln sub-summit).
pro_needs: No technical rock pro on the standard line; an ice axe is useful for early-season snow in the approach gullies.
rack: 30m rope + a few slings (optional, for the Class 4/low-5th chockstone move near the summit)

detailed_rack: Standard glacier-travel kit for the Blue Glacier/Hoh Glacier crossing: rope-team gear, harness, crevasse-rescue kit (prusiks or mechanical ascenders, pulley, cordage), ice axe, crampons, and a helmet (required). No technical rock rack is typically carried — the Class 4 ridge above the col/snow finger is generally scrambled unroped by parties comfortable with the exposure and loose rock.
pro_needs: Minimal fixed protection is used; the summit ridge is Class 4 scrambling, generally climbed unroped. The mandatory gear is for the approach: rope, harness, and crevasse-rescue kit for the Blue Glacier and Hoh Glacier crossings.

detailed_rack: Ice screws and pickets for the icefall's short vertical steps and ramps between crevasses, two ice tools, plus a light rock rack (small-to-medium cams/nuts) for the ~900 ft of 4th/low-5th class rock above - though protection on the rock is scarce due to crumbly rock quality, and many parties rely on running belays rather than placed gear.
pro_needs: Bring both ice and rock protection; the upper rock is poor quality so don't expect reliable placements - running belays are common practice here.
what_to_bring: approach shoes/boots suited to loose 4th class rock
check recent trip reports for current icefall condition before attempting

detailed_rack: A rope (30 m or longer) and a small rack of stoppers, a few pitons and slings: the roughly 25 ft 5.2 pitch below the summit is led, and both rappels come off anchors you build yourself. Ice axe useful early season.
pro_needs: Small rack of stoppers, a few pitons and slings for the 5.2 pitch and the rappel anchors
what_to_bring: extra food for the long approach

detailed_rack: Not a roped rock climb for most parties, but glacier and steep-snow gear is standard: ice axe, crampons, and helmet for the Royal Pass slope and Mystery Glacier; some parties carry a 30m rope and a few pickets/small rack (e.g., a couple of nuts) for the steep snow descent and as a bail option at the notch below the summit.
pro_needs: No technical rock pro required on the standard line; a short rope and a light alpine rack are sometimes carried for the exposed Class 3 summit moves and for belaying less-experienced partners.
rack: A couple of nuts and pickets (optional bail/protection option at the notch)

detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard Class 2+ scramble to Noyes' summit — it is unroped talus/scree travel. Carry an ice axe (and crampons if the snow is firm) for the steep snowfield guarding the approach col, especially early season.
pro_needs: None for the summit scramble itself. Parties continuing the connecting ridge toward Mount Meany should carry a rope (a 30m rope was used in one documented account) and minimal protection for the roped downclimb/rappel on that harder link, which is a separate undertaking from the standard Noyes route.
what_to_bring: Ice axe and light crampons for lingering snow in the cols, even in July
Wilderness camping permit (reserve on Recreation.gov) and a bear canister
Full multi-day backpacking kit — this is a 4-6 day wilderness expedition, not a day scramble
Map/compass or GPS for the unmaintained off-trail section above Low Divide

detailed_rack: No fixed technical rack is required — this is a scramble, not a roped rock route. Most parties carry an ice axe and crampons for the entry gully's snow rather than rock protection. Groups wanting extra security for the short loose class 4 rock step or the exposed summit knife-edge sometimes bring a 30-40m rope with a handful of slings/runners to rig a hip-belay or a quick sling-rappel off a horn, block, or tree; a light rack of nuts/small cams is optional insurance, not standard practice.
pro_needs: No fixed technical rock protection on the standard line, but the short Class 4 step and 45–50° snow gully lead most parties to carry an ice axe and crampons, and some carry a short rope for the crux step.
rack: 1-2 runners (optional handline on the exposed ridge section)

detailed_rack: Not a roped rock climb in summer conditions; parties typically carry an ice axe and, in early season, crampons or snowshoes for the upper mountain, plus a helmet for the loose rock band below the summit ridge. A short scramble rope is sometimes recommended for the Class 2/3 step for less experienced parties.
what_to_bring: Map/compass or GPS track (bootpath is easy to lose)
Extra water — little reliable water on route
Bug protection for brushy sections in summer

detailed_rack: No technical rack needed for the standard summer trail — it is a non-technical hike with a class 2-3 boulder scramble at the top. When snow lingers on the upper mountain (common into June, and again after early fall storms), carry an ice axe and traction devices (microspikes or crampons) for the steep boulder field and summit block.
pro_needs: No protection/pro needed in dry conditions; the only real technical consideration is footing on wet or icy granite in the boulder field and on the final scramble/ladder to the lookout.
what_to_bring: Northwest Forest Pass (or America the Beautiful interagency pass) to park at the trailhead
Extra water — no reliable water sources on the upper mountain
Layers and a rain shell for the exposed, weather-facing summit
Headlamp, given how many parties start late due to trailhead crowding

detailed_rack: No fixed protection; an ice axe is useful for the Price Creek gully and upper ridge when snow-covered, and a rope/light rack could be carried by less experienced parties for the steeper ridge sections, though most parties scramble it unroped.
pro_needs: None fixed — unroped scramble; steep snow sections may warrant an axe and, in early season, crampons/microspikes.
what_to_bring: Map/GPS with a saved track (routefinding is difficult and reported unreliable even with GPS)
Extra layers/food for a long day
Gaiters (boggy, brushy trail sections near the lakes)
Northwest Forest Pass / America the Beautiful Pass
Free self-issue wilderness permit (Alpine Lakes Wilderness, May 15-Oct 31)

detailed_rack: No rack. The published protection entry for Pika Slab reads "None" and the route carries an R rating precisely because nothing goes in. If you want the climb protected you must bring the means to rig it from above — a single rope, a couple of long slings and a few cams or nuts for whatever natural features you can find on the ledge or in the blocks above it, plus a belay device and a personal anchor. No fixed anchors are listed, so do not plan around finding bolts. Most parties who climb it simply solo the 20 feet in approach shoes and downclimb right.
pro_needs: Effectively none is placeable on the slab itself — this is a no-gear R-rated 20-footer, so the protection decision is binary: solo it, or build something from above and top-rope it. There is no middle ground and no reasonable lead protection.
what_to_bring: 3-4 litres of water per person — Lake Metan at 1.5 miles is the last reliable source, everything above is dry
Water filter or treatment for refilling at Lake Metan
Headlamp with fresh batteries (the descent routinely runs long)
Sun protection — the upper ridge is fully exposed with no shade
Wind shell and warm layer; the crest catches everything
Map, compass and downloaded GPS track — multiple braided boot paths on the upper ridge
First aid kit including trauma dressings appropriate to a rockfall/fall injury
Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle
Insect repellent for the forested lower trail in early summer

detailed_rack: No technical rack needed; ice axe useful when snow lingers on the upper ridge.
pro_needs: None for the standard scramble.
what_to_bring: 3-3.5+ liters of water (nothing reliable past Lake Metan)
ice axe (useful even in summer for the snowfield below the ridge crest)
helmet for the loose upper ridge
trekking poles for the steep switchbacks
sun protection - the upper mountain is fully exposed

detailed_rack: No fixed technical rock rack is standard for the East Ridge scramble itself. Because Pulitzer is only reached via the Bailey Range Traverse, parties carry full glacier travel kit for the approach: crampons, ice axe, a glacier rope, and basic crevasse-rescue hardware (e.g., Tibloc/Micro Traxion) for crossing Bailey Range snowfields and glaciers such as the one on Pulitzer's own north slope and Humes Glacier further south.
pro_needs: No fixed protection is placed on the standard scramble route; a small nut set has been carried by some parties for the loose, exposed final ridge to the true summit but is not standard gear for most ascents (many parties decline that section entirely).
rack: Small nut set (optional, carried by some parties for the loose, exposed final ridge to the true summit)
Glacier rope + crevasse-rescue hardware (Tibloc/Micro Traxion) for Bailey Range glacier crossings

detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard scramble line; the terrain is unroped class 2-3 scrambling with a snow-slope crossing near the top. Less experienced parties sometimes carry a light rope, harness and a picket or two for the snow slope, but most climbers travel unroped throughout.
pro_needs: Protection needs are minimal and informal: an ice axe (self-arrest) for the summit snow slope is the main 'protection' most parties carry; a rope/picket is optional insurance for less-experienced climbers on that slope only.
what_to_bring: bear canister (required NPS-wide in Olympic Wilderness)
map/compass or GPS for cross-country routefinding
extra food/fuel buffer for weather or route-finding delays on this multi-day approach
satellite communicator or PLB (no cell coverage)

detailed_rack: Light and fast: a helmet is essential in the loose crux gully; carry a 30m rope, harness, and a few slings only as a rappel option if descending the harder (Custer-to-Rahm) direction, since the gully's anchor quality is reportedly poor and untested.
pro_needs: Minimal — this is an unroped scramble except for a possible short rappel of the Class 4 crux gully when traveling Custer-to-Rahm.
what_to_bring: 30m rope, harness, and a few runners/slings in case the crux gully needs a rappel (Custer-to-Rahm direction; anchor quality reported as loose)

detailed_rack: No rack is needed for protection — this is an unroped scramble. Bring a helmet for the crux gully (a rockfall channel), and in early season an ice axe plus lightweight crampons for the steep upper-basin snowfield.
pro_needs: None — the crux gully is short (about 40 ft) and typically climbed without protection; a helmet is the main safety item.
what_to_bring: Trekking poles for the talus sections
A short hand-line/rope can help on a wet 8-ft rock step below Depot Creek Falls during the approach
Water treatment for camp at Ouzel or Silver Lake

detailed_rack: Standard glacier rope team of 2–4. Per person: ice axe, 12-point crampons, helmet, harness, prusiks/ascender, 2–3 locking carabiners, belay device. Per rope team: 30–40 m glacier rope, 2–4 pickets, a couple of ice screws for late-season crevasse spanning, crevasse-rescue pulley kit.
pro_needs: Protection is glacier-travel oriented — pickets and the occasional ice screw for running belays across crevasse zones rather than rock pro.

detailed_rack: Glacier rope team kit: 30–40 m rope per team, 2–4 pickets, crevasse-rescue gear (pulleys, prusiks), 1–2 ice screws late season. Per person: ice axe, crampons, helmet, harness, locking biners.
pro_needs: Glacier protection only — pickets and screws for running belays through crevasse zones and the steeper upper slopes.
what_to_bring: stove for melting water at Schurman

detailed_rack: Standard glacier kit with a couple of pickets for the steeper couloir; helmet essential for rockfall. Ski crampons useful for ski parties.
pro_needs: Glacier travel gear; pickets for the steeper snow

detailed_rack: Glacier kit with pickets for the couloir; helmet essential for rockfall.
pro_needs: Pickets and team arrest; no technical rock gear normally required.

detailed_rack: Glacier kit plus a couple of pickets and an ice screw or two for the Gibraltar Chute; helmet mandatory for the rockfall-prone ledges.
pro_needs: Pickets; the ledge traverse can require care when icy

detailed_rack: Standard glacier rope team of 2–4. Per person: ice axe, 12-point crampons, helmet, harness, prusiks/ascender, 2–3 locking carabiners, belay device. Per rope team: 30–40 m glacier rope, 2–4 pickets, a couple of ice screws for late-season crevasse spanning, crevasse-rescue pulley kit.
pro_needs: Protection is glacier-travel oriented — pickets and the occasional ice screw for running belays across crevasse zones rather than rock pro.

detailed_rack: Per person: ice axe plus a second technical tool, 12-point crampons, helmet, harness. Per rope team: 60 m rope, 4–6 ice screws (for the chute), 2–4 pickets, crevasse-rescue kit, a couple of slings/cordelettes for V-thread or picket anchors.
pro_needs: Mixed glacier + ice protection: screws for the ice steps, pickets for snow, plus standard crevasse-rescue gear. No rock pro needed.

detailed_rack: Same core glacier/ice rack as the standard Kautz Glacier route: 2-4 ice screws per person, several pickets, 2 small pulleys and 2 prussiks per climber for crevasse rescue, helmet, and a harness/belay-rappel device.
pro_needs: Ice screws and pickets for the steep headwall
rack: 2 small pulleys + 2 prusiks per climber (crevasse rescue)

detailed_rack: Per person: two technical ice tools, 12-point crampons, helmet, harness. Per team: 30–60 m rope (often two for rappels), 4–6 ice screws, 2–3 pickets, a light rock rack (small cams/nuts) for the Black Pyramid, V-thread tool, crevasse-rescue kit.
pro_needs: Mixed: ice screws and pickets for the steep snow/ice, a small rock rack for the Black Pyramid section, and anchors for rappelling the bergschrund/upper headwall on retreat.

detailed_rack: No technical rack; ice axe useful early season for snow on the approach slopes.
pro_needs: None.

detailed_rack: A light glacier/snow rack: 1-2 pickets, an ice axe, crampons, and a rope for the glacier crossing and the exposed traverse beneath the summit; a small rock rack is optional for the Class 3 ridge step.
pro_needs: Snow protection (pickets/flukes) for the Wall Street couloir and the glacier-bowl traverse beneath the summit; a rope is commonly used for both the glacier crossing and the exposed Class 3 ridge traverse.
what_to_bring: Light rock rack for the Class 3 ridge step (optional)
Sun protection for the glacier crossing
Extra layers — the saddle and ridge are wind-exposed

detailed_rack: Two ice axes, crampons, 6-8 ice screws, picket(s), full crevasse rescue setup
pro_needs: Ice screws and pickets for steep ice and serac terrain
rack: Light rack to 2in cams, small nut set for the 5.6 summit pyramid finish

detailed_rack: Two ice axes, crampons, 6-8 ice screws, 2-3 pickets, small rock rack for mixed sections, full crevasse rescue setup including pulleys and carabiners
pro_needs: Ice screws, pickets, and a light rack for the summit pyramid
rack: Small rock rack (few cams/hexes), few nuts

detailed_rack: No technical rack is needed for the standard scramble; an ice axe (and light crampons in early season) substitute for gear on the upper snow/gully sections.
pro_needs: No technical rock pro on the standard line; an ice axe is useful for early-season snow in the gullies.

detailed_rack: Standard glacier travel kit (rope, harness, crevasse-rescue gear) for crossing the Silver Glacier, plus a small rock rack and runners/slings to protect the short Class 4 step below the summit.
pro_needs: A small rack and a few runners are enough to protect the short Class 4 summit step; the bulk of the route's difficulty is glacier travel rather than sustained rock climbing.
what_to_bring: Ross Lake Resort water-taxi reservation if using the Silver Creek approach
North Cascades NP wilderness permit for camping
Ross Dam Trailhead Trail Park Pass if driving to Ross Lake

detailed_rack: Summer: no technical gear — sturdy boots, gloves for the boulder scramble, trekking poles. Winter/spring: ice axe and crampons for the snow slopes; helmet advisable. No rope or rock pro on the standard route.
pro_needs: None — Monitor Ridge is a permitted scramble/snow climb, not a roped route.

detailed_rack: Winter/spring snow climb: ice axe and crampons per person, helmet, trekking poles. Carry avalanche safety gear (beacon, probe, shovel) and know how to use it. No rope/rock pro on the standard route.
pro_needs: None technical — but avalanche assessment and self-arrest skills are essential.

detailed_rack: Helmets are essential due to loose Olympic basalt and rockfall hazard. Ice axes recommended for travel June-July when snow and ice patches are common. Microspikes useful for frozen snow. Trekking poles recommended for steep descent on Putvin Trail.
pro_needs: Rock scrambling experience, comfortable with exposure, navigation skills (map, compass, GPS). Helmets recommended due to rockfall hazard and loose rock common to Olympic basalt.
what_to_bring: 10 essentials (map, compass, sunscreen, first aid, knife, fire starter, shelter, extra clothes, extra food, extra water)
Backpack (20-25L for day hike, 40L+ for overnight)

detailed_rack: Non-technical in summer: helmet (rockfall), sturdy boots, trekking poles. Early season add ice axe and possibly crampons for couloir snow. No rope required for the standard line, though some parties bring a short rope for the summit block.
pro_needs: None on the standard scramble; a short rope is optional for nervous parties on the summit block.
what_to_bring: Ice axe and crampons if climbing before the couloir melts out (commonly into June)
Northwest Forest Pass / Interagency pass for trailhead parking
Self-issue wilderness permit (fill out at the trailhead)

detailed_rack: Single to double rack of cams through hand size, a set of nuts, plus ice axe and crampons for the glacier approach and descent.
pro_needs: Standard alpine rack emphasizing finger-to-hand cracks; light glacier kit for the approach.

detailed_rack: Per person: two technical ice tools, crampons, helmet, harness. Per team: 30–60 m rope, 6–8 ice screws, 2–4 pickets, a light rock rack for the mixed exit, V-thread/rappel kit, crevasse-rescue gear.
pro_needs: Steep-ice and mixed protection — screws for the ice cliff bypass, pickets for snow, a little rock pro for the exit. Full glacier/crevasse capability.

detailed_rack: Single rack of cams from small to ~3 inches, a set of nuts, 8–10 alpine draws/slings, a 60 m rope (or twins for rappels), helmet, and crevasse/snow gear for the glacier approach. Some parties bring a light second rope for the descent rappels.
pro_needs: Standard alpine rock rack — the Great Gendarme is the protection crux (thin to hand cracks). Glacier-travel gear needed for the approach.

detailed_rack: Light alpine rack: a few nuts and small-to-medium cams, alpine draws, a 60 m rope, helmet. Much of the ridge is 3rd/4th class with short 5th-class steps, so a minimal rack suffices for confident parties.
pro_needs: Minimal rock pro for the short 5.4 steps and the False Summit area; mostly a roped scramble for many parties.

detailed_rack: No technical protection rack is used — this is an unroped scramble route; microspikes or light traction may be warranted for lingering snow near the ridge crest.
pro_needs: None; sure footing and caution on wet rock substitute for any climbing protection.
what_to_bring: layers for wind/exposure on the ridge
headlamp in case of a late finish

detailed_rack: A standard alpine rock rack (cams and stoppers to ~3in, several slings/draws) covers the technical ground; add ice axe, crampons, and glacier travel gear (rope, pickets/screws as conditions dictate) for the Ottohorn-Himmel col and Mustard Glacier crossing.
pro_needs: Protection is moderate for the grade — mid-size cams and stoppers protect the cracks and dihedrals on the traverse, with natural gear/slung horns useful near the crux chimney; the rock is described as generally solid but with isolated loose blocks.
rack: Cams and stoppers to 3in (medium sizes for the offwidth section)
Ice axe, crampons, thin glacier rope for the Mustard Glacier approach

detailed_rack: Alpine rock rack, glacier-travel gear (axe/crampons) for the approach col and glacier, and a 60m rope; some parties have also carried a machete for approach brush.
pro_needs: Standard alpine rack with doubles in finger-to-hand sizes for the sustained low-5th crest pitches; protection thins out on the knife-edge finish, so be comfortable running it out on solid rock there.
what_to_bring: Bivy/camp gear for the multi-day approach

detailed_rack: A short rope, a piton or two, and a basic light rock rack are enough for the short technical section; a helmet is essential given the loose rock throughout.
pro_needs: Minimal gear is needed — the crux crack above the notch takes small-to-medium gear and an occasional piton placement; most of the route is unprotected scrambling.

detailed_rack: ["Cams roughly 0.5\"-2\" (a handful of small-to-mid sizes covers most placements)", "Set of nuts/stoppers", "About 6 alpine quickdraws/slings (most pitches take only 3-4 placements)", "Ice axe useful if early-season snow lingers on the approach/basin"]
pro_needs: Light natural protection and minimal aid gear needed. The route is well-anchored on natural features. No bolts or fixed anchors on the route; all belay stations are at natural ledges with bomber rock for anchor placement (trees, blocks, cracks).

detailed_rack: Full glacier mountaineering rack: ice axe and crampons per climber (most parties use half-rope or simul-roped techniques on Blue Glacier). For White Glacier ascent, bring standard rock protection (nuts, cams size 0-2) for potential runner anchors in Class 3 sections, though many parties climb unroped on well-established scramble terrain. Pickets or snow anchors for glacier belays.
pro_needs: Solid understanding of self-rescue on glaciers, ability to identify and cross crevasse fields, competence with ice axe braking, and proficiency with Class 3 rock. Parties should include at least one person experienced with crevasse rescue and rope management.
rack: Ice axe and crampons per climber
Crevasse rescue kit (pulley, prusiks, cordelette, 4 locking biners)
Team rope for Blue Glacier crossing (not a lead rope)
Optional cams/nuts 0-2 for occasional Class 3 runner anchors
Pickets or snow anchors for glacier belays
what_to_bring: Rope, pickets/screws, and a crevasse-rescue kit for glacier travel
Light rock rack (small nuts/cams) for the summit scramble in case the harder variation is encountered
Satellite communicator or PLB (no cell coverage)
Water treatment (fords and glacier melt streams en route)

detailed_rack: A single rack of cams from 0.4 to 2 inches, a set of nuts, about 8 alpine draws with slings for towers, and a 60m rope. Add ice axe and crampons for the glacier approach.
pro_needs: The granite protects well on the steeper steps with cracks and horns, with run-out moderate sections between. Slinging towers speeds protection on the exposed crest.

detailed_rack: A single rack of cams from 0.4 to 2 inches, a set of nuts, about 8 alpine draws with slings, and two ropes for the rappels. Carry ice axe and crampons for the snow sections.
pro_needs: Protection on the rock steps is reasonable, but much of the traverse is moderate, exposed, run-out terrain where efficient movement matters more than gear. The snow sections take occasional pickets.

detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is typically carried — this is done as an unroped scramble by essentially all parties. A helmet is strongly advised given the loose Olympic rock, and an ice axe may be warranted for early-season snow patches on the approach.
pro_needs: Standard route is unroped Class 3-4 scrambling for confident parties; a rope, harness, and a few slings/small rack add security on the short steeper steps for less-experienced scramblers.
what_to_bring: Ice axe if snow lingers in the gullies (common into early July)
Bear canister for overnight camps in Royal Basin
Map/compass or GPS — gully route-finding is easy to get wrong

detailed_rack: No technical climbing rack required. Ice axe (60-70cm) essential for early season (May-June) or late season (Sept-Oct) when snow may be present; recommended even in summer for self-arrest capability. Helmet strongly recommended for rockfall and scrambling accidents. Trekking poles provide stability on loose terrain.
pro_needs: No technical rock pro required on the standard line; early season an ice axe and snow-travel skills are important for the upper gully.
what_to_bring: Sturdy boots for scree/talus and rock steps
Sun protection (limited shade above the talus field)

detailed_rack: Pickets and a small assortment of cams/nuts for the rock/snow crux pitch, plus two ice tools (one more technical, one piolet-style).
pro_needs: Mixed snow and rock protection: pickets for the snow, a small rack for the chossy rock section.

detailed_rack: Not a roped rock climb for most parties; carry a lightweight ice axe and crampons (or aggressive microspikes) for the snow/glacier notch, plus a helmet for the loose, mossy scrambling along the ridge west of the col and the exposed summit ridge. Some parties carry a short rope/basic glacier gear for the small Watson Glacier remnant depending on conditions.
pro_needs: No fixed protection or rappel stations are documented; this is unroped class 3 scrambling with one short, steep snow/glacier crossing. A rope is optional insurance for the glacier apron in early season, not standard gear for most summer ascents.
what_to_bring: Ice axe (recommended into July for the saddle/gully)
Sturdy boots for talus and scrambling
DEET-free insect repellent (lakes are notoriously buggy)
Optional short hand line/webbing for the exposed summit block
Northwest Forest Pass for the trailhead

detailed_rack: No technical rock gear for the standard scramble; ice axe early season
pro_needs: None for the standard line

detailed_rack: No rock rack is needed. The standard line is a Class 2-3 scramble up heather and blocky rock; what is left of the Mutchler Glacier clings only to the highest north-facing slopes, and parties reach the summit unroped, so an ice axe for lingering snow is the only technical gear to carry.
pro_needs: No protection is needed on the standard line: it is a Class 2-3 scramble with no roped glacier travel, and there are no fixed anchors or bolts on the scrambling sections.
what_to_bring: extra food/water for a long day

detailed_rack: At minimum an ice axe is required; if the snow is continuous, a rope with medium nuts and/or pickets is recommended for protection, particularly through the steeper mid- and upper-couloir sections.
pro_needs: An ice axe is essential. If the snow is continuous, bring a rope and medium nuts and pickets for protection of the crux section.
what_to_bring: Rope + snow protection if conditions warrant
Early alpine start to catch firm snow

detailed_rack: A light rack of nuts and several long slings suffices for the brief 5.3 sections; a helmet is recommended for the loose scrambling terrain.
pro_needs: Minimal protection needed — mostly scrambling with only a couple of protectable 5.3 moves per pitch.
rack: Single dynamic rope (for the brief 5.3 moves on each pitch)
what_to_bring: Map and compass or GPS (long trail approach)

detailed_rack: A 30m rope and a few slings cover a crux move or short rappel; ice axe for early-season snow on the Swamp Creek basin approach.

No technical rock rack is required — every documented ascent is an unroped scramble. Bring a helmet for the loose rock in the upper cliff bands and gully, trekking poles for the brushy lower approach, and a light ice axe if snow lingers in the gullies early in the season.
pro_needs: Minimal rack — a light rope plus a few slings/small pieces to back up or replace the crux notch anchor; this is a scramble with a short technical crux, not a pitched rock climb.
rack: 30m rope for the 5.0 crux notch downclimb/rappel
2x 60cm webbing for the rap anchor/handline at the crux
A few small slings/pieces to back up the anchor
what_to_bring: NPS wilderness permit (reserved or self-issued) for the park/NRA portion of the approach
Overnight camping gear for Swamp Creek Camp
Extra water — camp sits well below the summit with no reliable water higher up
Insect repellent (wasp activity reported on the approach)
Topo map/GPS track — the route is unmarked and unmaintained beyond Swamp Creek Camp
Satellite messenger — no cell coverage in the valley or on route

detailed_rack: Small-to-medium cam set (~0.3-2in) plus a stopper set covers the knob/crack protection, with 4-6 quickdraws for the bolted sections and slings for slinging knobs and horns, a traditional protection style at this crag before bolts were added; helmet is mandatory given loose welded-tuff cobbles.
what_to_bring: Approach shoes for the road walk-in

detailed_rack: No rope or rack is used; this is a crampon-and-axe snow/scree scramble, not a roped climb.
