what_to_bring: A plan or footwear for a cold ford of Cedar Creek
A GPS or downloaded track — there is no maintained trail for much of the route

detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is used on this route — it is climbed as an unroped Class 2-3 scramble. Trekking poles are widely recommended for the steep, loose scree sections; an ice axe may be prudent if lingering snow remains on north-facing terrain earlier in the season.
pro_needs: None — parties do not typically place protection or use a rope on this line; it is treated as advanced scrambling terrain throughout.

detailed_rack: No fixed protection and generally no roped rock pitches for parties comfortable soloing loose 3rd/4th class; ice axe and crampons are the core tools for the snow fins below the summit block.
pro_needs: A light rock rack is optional insurance for less experienced parties on the final loose scrambling, but the route is normally climbed unroped on the rock.
rack: Single 30-40m rope for short-roping/belaying exposed sections (especially on descent)
Optional light rack (0.5-2in cams, small nut set, 2 slings) only if straying onto 4th-class terrain
what_to_bring: glacier travel gear if linking with a Whatcom Glacier descent/ascent
trekking poles for the multi-day approach
sturdy boots for scree/talus and loose rock

detailed_rack: A light alpine rock rack (small-to-medium cams and stoppers) is sufficient for the low-5th-class climbing on the ridge's generally good but locally loose rock. Carry standard glacier travel gear (axe, crampons, rope, pickets) for the approach glacier, and a rope for rappelling the ridge if retreat is needed.
pro_needs: Gear is placed sparingly on this short ridge; small cams and stoppers protect the low-5th-class sections, supplemented by natural gear (slings over blocks/horns) — it is trad-only, with no fixed/bolted protection reported.
rack: Small-to-mid rack: cams to 2-3in, nut set
what_to_bring: Bivy/overnight gear for the multi-day approach
GPS track — the route is lightly documented and easy to lose
Extra cord/rope in case the ridge must be rappelled to retreat

detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard scramble. Carry an ice axe (and consider crampons in early season) for the Spider Gap snowfield/glacier crossing if approaching via Phelps Creek, plus a helmet for the loose talus and the Class 3 summit block.
pro_needs: None — this is an unroped scramble. The main terrain concern is the permanent snowfield/moat near 7,000 ft on the Spider Gap approach, which some parties treat with an ice axe for self-arrest.
what_to_bring: Ice axe (and consider light traction) for lingering snow at Spider Gap and the upper basin into August
Helmet for loose talus and rockfall
Free self-issue wilderness permit (fill out at the trailhead register)
Overnight gear — realistically a 2-4 day trip from either trailhead
Green Trails Holden No. 113 map and solid navigation skills — no maintained summit trail
Satellite communicator — no cell coverage in this basin

detailed_rack: Not a roped rock route for most parties: sturdy scrambling boots and a helmet are the core kit. Early-season parties carry an ice axe and crampons for lingering snow on the ridge and for the optional north-face glissade descent. A handful of parties bring a light rack and a short rope for the optional M1b mixed variation start or for the class 5 moves near the Cockscomb if climbing with less-experienced partners.
pro_needs: Protection needs are minimal on the standard class 3-4 line; a light rack (a few cams/nuts and slings) covers the short M1b variation start or any roped class 5 moves near the Cockscomb for parties who choose to belay them.
rack: Optional light rack: a few small cams/nuts for the M1b mixed variation start or Class 5 crest moves
Webbing, quick-links/rap rings for rap stations
70m half rope, harness, belay device, prusik (carried by parties tackling the harder options)
Ice axe, crampons for early-season snow/glissade descent
what_to_bring: Hampton Family Forests non-motorized recreation permit (buy it before driving out and carry it printed)
GPX track or a detailed written road-fork description - the logging-road maze is the single biggest cause of lost time
Mountain bike, to cut hours off the ~5-6 mile road approach
Plenty of water - little to no reliable water source once you leave the lower road system

detailed_rack: A standard alpine rock rack to 3 inches with doubles of 0.5-2 for the dihedral and corner pitches, plus a few extra slings for the wandering, zig-zag line. Carry light aluminum crampons and a light axe (or whippet) for the glacier crossing, not for the technical climbing.
pro_needs: Protection is intermittent on some traversing pitches; doubles of the smaller-to-mid cam sizes (0.5-2) see the most use in the dihedral and corner systems.
what_to_bring: extra layers for a long day

detailed_rack: Crampons, a 60m or 70m rope, ice axe, a single set of cams from about 0.3-3 in (e.g. BD Camelots), a set of nuts, a few small Mastercams, a helmet, and 2 pickets.
pro_needs: A single light rack (cams 0.3-3in, nuts, a few small Mastercams) covers the 5.6 rock; 2 pickets and an ice axe/crampons cover the couloir and glacier; an anchored belay is recommended for crossing the moat at the top of the glacier.
what_to_bring: topographic map and compass (cell coverage unreliable)

detailed_rack: A small-to-medium alpine rock rack up to about 3 inches, 10+ runners/slings, plus ice axe and crampons for the couloir/glacier portion of the approach.
pro_needs: Standard alpine rock rack to 3 inches with plenty of runners for the 12-pitch rib; supplement with snow/ice protection for the lower couloir approach.
rack: Ice axe, crampons for the couloir/glacier approach
what_to_bring: light bivy gear as a contingency

detailed_rack: A medium alpine rock rack up to 3+ inches with 8-10 runners covers the route; a helmet is essential given loose rock in places.
pro_needs: Protection is variable — the opening pitch (5.8+) is not greatly protected, and the crux corner/chimney relies in part on a single fixed pin.
rack: Medium alpine rack to 3in, including a #4 Camalot for pitch 1
what_to_bring: bivy gear if splitting the route over two days
approach shoes for the Bedal basin hike

detailed_rack: Small rack to 2.5 inches (cams and nuts), ice axe, crampons, and about 6 ft of extra webbing for the rappel anchor.
pro_needs: Light rack — small-to-mid cams and nuts suffice for the short ridge pitches; slings for horn anchors.
what_to_bring: Mountaineering boots (many parties climb the whole route in boots rather than carrying rock shoes)

detailed_rack: A light alpine rack suffices for 5.6 ridge climbing on granodiorite: a single set of cams roughly from small to #2 Camalot, a set of nuts, a good number of long slings for the ridge's horns and blocks, and a 60 m rope, which also covers the 25 m descent rappel. Bring a cordelette and some spare tat for building or backing up belays and the rappel anchor. Helmets throughout — the gully and the talus descent are loose. Before mid-July add an ice axe and traction for the approach gully and the descent slopes.
pro_needs: Minimal and mostly slung. The sharp ridge takes long slings over horns and blocks more than it takes cam placements, so weight the rack toward runners. A single set of cams and nuts covers the occasional crack. The only place where protection genuinely matters is the summit block itself, which is a short but seriously exposed V1 boulder problem — most parties belay it rather than solo it.
rack: Light trad rack (small-to-medium cams and nuts)
Single 60 m rope (covers the ~25 m descent rappel)
what_to_bring: Helmet — the gully and the talus descent are loose
Approach shoes or light boots for the trail, gully and talus
2-3 L water capacity and a filter; Colchuck Lake is the last reliable water
Wind shell and warm layer for an exposed northwest ridge
Ice axe and microspikes before mid-July
Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass

detailed_rack: Standard glacier-travel kit: ice axe, crampons, a rope per team, pickets or ice screws, and a full crevasse-rescue kit (prusiks, pulley, mechanical ascenders), plus a helmet for the scramble above the col. No technical rock rack is used on this class 2-3 route.
pro_needs: None beyond glacier-travel protection - pickets/screws for crevasse rescue and a belay on the snow ramp if desired; the summit scramble itself is unroped class 2-3.

detailed_rack: No rack is needed — this is an unroped scramble. Trekking poles are widely used and typically stashed just below the final scramble; in early season (persistent snow on the PCT sidehill traverse and the climb up to the summit path) an ice axe and microspikes/traction devices are commonly carried for self-arrest and secure footing.
pro_needs: No technical protection is used on the standard route — it is a trail hike to a Class 2–3 scramble finish. Trekking poles are commonly carried for the snowfields and loose talus.

detailed_rack: Ice axe and crampons for the glacier approach (rope up for crevasse hazard); helmet; a few small-to-medium cams and nuts with slings for the summit pyramid; a 30m+ rope doubles as glacier rope and rappel line if descending the east-side dihedral (two rope-length rappels reported).
pro_needs: Light rack (small-to-medium cams/nuts) for the class 4 summit pyramid, plus a standard glacier travel kit (axe, crampons, rope) for the Overcoat Glacier approach.
what_to_bring: Helmet, ice axe, crampons for glacier travel
Light rock rack (small-medium cams/nuts, slings) for the summit pyramid
Satellite communicator (inReach/SPOT) — little to no cell coverage along the approach
Water treatment and bug protection for camp

detailed_rack: No rope or protection is used on the standard route; it is an off-trail Class 3 scramble. A helmet is recommended for the short ledge band above the trail's end, and an ice axe (with self-arrest skills) is essential if snow lingers on the upper ridge or summit slopes.
pro_needs: None — no roped protection is placed on this route. Helmet for the loose ledge band; ice axe/crampons only if snow is present on the upper mountain.
what_to_bring: Helmet (rockfall risk on the exposed ledges)
Trekking poles for the scree sections
Map/compass or GPS -- the route is unsigned and unmaintained past mile 1
3+ liters of water (limited reliable sources en route)
Sun protection for the open ridge and summit slopes

detailed_rack: Minimal gear typically used: selection of nuts (black diamond size range), several slings. No ice screws or technical tools needed, but crampons, an ice axe and 3-4 snow pickets or flukes are required for the snow finger and bergschrund.
pro_needs: Snow flukes for bergschrund area and steep slopes. Small emergency kit given remote location and lack of cell service.
rack: Light rack: a few nuts and slings for anchors
Glacier travel kit: rope, crevasse-rescue hardware
what_to_bring: Bug head-net — flies are a serious nuisance in Luna Cirque through July
Bear canister or Ursack for food storage

detailed_rack: No technical climbing gear (rope, rack, harness) is used on this route — it is an unroped, off-trail scramble. In the snow-covered conditions most parties prefer (roughly Nov-Jun), bring an ice axe and microspikes or snowshoes for the boulder field and upper ridge; several parties describe stashing snowshoes around 3,000-3,400 ft once the ridge crest firms up. Trekking poles help through the brushy, blown-down lower ridge in bare-ground conditions.
what_to_bring: Map, compass, and/or a GPS track — no maintained trail or cairns beyond Lake Serene
Gaiters and brush-tolerant clothing for the slide alder and salmonberry
Northwest Forest Pass for the trailhead
Snowshoes and an ice axe for Nov-Apr ascents

detailed_rack: A standard alpine trad rack: a single set of cams from small to about 3 inches (rock is generally sound and takes gear well on the upper pitches), a set of stoppers, and a handful of slings/draws. The first pitch is notably underprotected — the first-ascent party placed only a single small cam in the first 20 feet — so extra small/marginal gear and a willingness to run it out should be expected. Glacier-travel gear (crevasse-rescue kit, harness, prusiks, crampons, axe) is required for the Challenger Glacier approach and descent.
pro_needs: Standard alpine rack; placements on the crux first pitch are sparse and small, so the pitch should be treated as effectively R-rated regardless of rack size.
what_to_bring: Satellite communicator (no cell service in the backcountry)
Sun protection for extended glacier travel
Food storage/bear canister per NPS wilderness permit requirements

detailed_rack: A standard alpine rock rack: cams from small to about 3 inches, a set of nuts, and extra slings for the corner and ledge pitches; rock is generally sound and takes gear well, except the first ~40 ft of the dike-streaked shield on pitch 1, which is essentially unprotectable. Add glacier travel gear (rope, crevasse-rescue kit, ice axe, crampons) for the Challenger Glacier crossing on approach and descent.
pro_needs: Gear anchors throughout — the rock is sound and protects well, except the first ~40 ft of pitch 1 across the dike shield, which takes essentially no gear. Fixed anchors (bolts) are prohibited across the surrounding Stephen Mather Wilderness, so retreat and belays rely entirely on removable protection.

detailed_rack: No technical rock or glacier gear is used on the standard route. Parties typically carry an ice axe and light traction (microspikes or crampons) for firm spring/early-summer snow on the upper ridge, plus standard off-trail navigation tools; no rope or protection is placed.
pro_needs: None — the standard route is an unroped scramble with no fixed anchors, rock protection, or belays on record.

detailed_rack: The standard through-traverse is a glacier/scramble route, not a pitched rock climb, so the 'rack' is mostly glacier-travel and crevasse-rescue kit rather than rock gear: ice axe, crampons (aluminum acceptable, some parties use lightweight strap-on models), climbing harness, helmet, and a shared rope — either a 30m 'glacier rope' per 2 people or a single lightweight 60m 8-9mm rope split among a 3-person team. Crevasse-rescue gear is the real 'rack' here: a pulley, 2-3 locking carabiners, 2 prusik cords (pre-rigged 'texas prusiks'/hero loops work well), a cordelette or 5.5mm accessory cord, and 1-2 snow pickets per rope team (add 1-2 lightweight aluminum ice screws, e.g. 21cm, if traveling late-season when the Le Conte Glacier can go bare-ice). No rock rack is needed for the standard route. If adding optional technical side-summits (Dome Peak's exposed class 3-4 final scramble, or a Sinister Peak side trip), bring a light rock rack: a half-set of nuts, a nut tool, a few small-to-mid cams (~0.1-2in) or tricams, and 3-4 shoulder-length slings for natural or gear anchors/short raps.
pro_needs: Protection needs are minimal and glacier-hazard-driven rather than rock-driven: pickets and (late-season) ice screws for crevasse-rescue anchors are the main 'pro' on this route, not cams/nuts. Rock protection only comes into play on optional side-summit scrambles (e.g. Dome Peak's final exposed step, occasionally belayed) or as a rappel backup if the Red Ledge traverse beneath Arts Knoll is broken by a melted-out gap (documented up to 15-20ft raps in some seasons) — the granite there is solid and takes gear fine, but placements are sparse because most parties simply scramble/hand-line rather than place traditional pro.
rack: Glacier rope (30m per rope team, or shared 60m 8-9mm rope for a 3-person team)
Crevasse-rescue kit: pulley, 2 prusik cords, cordelette, 2-3 lockers
Optional light rock rack for side-summits: half-set of nuts, small-to-mid cams (~0.1-2in), 3-4 slings
what_to_bring: multi-day pack with camp gear (tent, stove, bear-resistant food storage) for the typical 4-7 day traverse
map/compass/GPS — extensive off-trail navigation across ~6 glaciers
1-2 lightweight aluminum ice screws if attempting late-season when the Le Conte Glacier can be bare ice

detailed_rack: No rock rack is needed for the standard scramble. Carry an ice axe (and crampons if attempting outside the July-September window) for lingering snow near the Pyramid-Pinnacle saddle. A rope is optional insurance some parties carry for the exposed traverse beneath the cliffs, but it is not standard practice on this route.
pro_needs: Mostly Class 3-4 scrambling; a short rope and a few slings are optional for the exposed summit steps.

detailed_rack: No fixed rack required for the boulder scramble from the col to the summit. Winter/spring ascents should carry standard ski-mountaineering and avalanche safety gear (beacon, probe, shovel).
pro_needs: None for the summer scramble; it is unroped throughout on the documented ascent.
what_to_bring: overnight camping gear if splitting the trip at Crater Lake

detailed_rack: No fixed protection or technical rack is needed for the standard scrambling line. A helmet is strongly recommended given the pervasive loose rock and rockfall risk in the ascent gully. Parties planning to continue the connecting ridge toward Hoodoo Peak (or wanting a safety net for the Class 4 summit move) sometimes carry a short 30–60 m rope or a sling, since a rappel station exists on that connector near a near-vertical step.
pro_needs: None fixed on the standard route; an optional short rope/sling covers the exposed Class 4 summit move or the Hoodoo Peak ridge connector.
what_to_bring: Detailed map/GPS — route-finding through the talus gully and along the ridge is nontrivial
Sun protection (little shade on the open ridge)
Extra water (few reliable sources above Libby Lake late in season)
Insect repellent (mosquitoes reported near Libby Lake and the old cabin)
Wind layers for the exposed summit ridge
Satellite communicator (no cell coverage confirmed in the field reports reviewed)

detailed_rack: No technical rack required. Helmet is the one piece of 'gear' that meaningfully changes the risk profile here given documented rockfall.
pro_needs: None — no rack, rope, or protection needed; this is unroped Class 2-3 scrambling on both standard lines.
what_to_bring: 2+ liters of water (no reliable water past the basin pond)
Sun protection — the upper slope is fully exposed
Layers for wind on the open summit

detailed_rack: Not a technical rock climb — most parties solo the Class 2-3 terrain, but a short (30m) rope with a few slings/runners is worth carrying to protect the exposed Class 3 step below the summit with a running belay. Early-season parties should carry an ice axe (and consider microspikes/light crampons) for the snow gully and approach snowfields.
pro_needs: Unroped class 2-3 scramble; no technical gear normally required.

detailed_rack: No rock rack is documented for the ridge. The approach along the traverse crosses crevassed glaciers, so the party needs a basic glacier kit: a rope, harnesses, crampons, ice axes and crevasse-rescue gear, plus helmets.
pro_needs: No protection is documented for the ridge crest itself, but the approach crosses crevassed glaciers, so carry a glacier rope, harnesses, crampons and ice axes.
what_to_bring: glacier rope, harness and crevasse-rescue kit

detailed_rack: No technical rack is needed for the standard ascent — this is an unroped scramble. A helmet is strongly recommended for the Class 2-3 knife-edge section (loose rock, real exposure), and an ice axe (with crampons in early season) for the snow slope below the ridge crest.
pro_needs: No technical protection required; this is an unroped class 2-3 scramble on talus/scree and broken ridge crest.
what_to_bring: large volume of water (little to none available above the tarn)
sun protection (hat, sunscreen, sunglasses - route is largely shadeless)
map/compass or GPS (route-finding experience required on unmarked Beauty Creek Trail and scree)
wilderness self-issue permit (fill out at trailhead)

detailed_rack: Not a roped climbing route; equipped as a ski-mountaineering ascent (skis/skins or splitboard, or snowshoes if not skiing) rather than with a technical rack.
what_to_bring: Extra traction for firm/icy morning snow
Sun protection for spring snow travel
Map/GPS — the upper bootpath is faint and route-finding depends partly on established tracks

detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard class 3 route. Depending on season, carry an ice axe (and crampons if snow lingers on the crest) plus a full off-trail/glacier-adjacent backpacking kit for the multi-day approach.
what_to_bring: Satellite communicator or PLB given the remote, off-trail setting
Extra water capacity for the dry stretch past Eleven Bull Basin toward Cream Lake
Sun protection — much of the Bailey Range travel is above treeline and exposed

detailed_rack: A standard glacier kit: ice axe, crampons, a glacier rope, a crevasse-rescue kit, and a few slings for the summit block. A helmet is recommended for the loose final scramble.
pro_needs: Protection is minimal, with standard glacier-travel anchors and a sling or two on the summit block. The route is about easy glacier travel and a short scramble rather than rock protection.

detailed_rack: Standard glacier mountaineering rack: one rope per rope team, a full crevasse-rescue kit (prusik cords or mechanical ascenders, pulleys, carabiners, an ice screw or picket for anchors), harness, helmet, ice axe, and crampons. No rock protection or pitched climbing gear is needed for the scramble sections; a single picket or ice screw for a crevasse-rescue anchor is the extent of placed protection most parties carry.
pro_needs: Roped glacier travel with crevasse-rescue capability is required to reach the peak; the summit rim itself is a short class 2-3 scramble.

detailed_rack: Glacier rope per rope team, pickets/ice screws for crevasse-rescue anchors, prusiks or mechanical ascenders, pulley and locking carabiners for rescue systems, crampons and ice axe for the steeper, icier upper slopes; front-pointing technique is required below the summit ridge in icy conditions.
pro_needs: Standard crevasse-rescue protection (pickets/screws); no rock protection is placed. Steeper icy sections near the top may warrant a second tool for some parties.
what_to_bring: Whippet or second tool for icy sections
Skis or snowshoes for the approach in shoulder-season conditions
Layered clothing for volcano weather swings

detailed_rack: Most parties solo the route early season; rope, axe, and crampons are standard, with rappel gear and snow/ice protection as a contingency once the glacier opens up later.
pro_needs: Minimal formal protection when climbed early season and solo; carry pickets/screws as the glacier deteriorates.
rack: A couple of ice screws (provisional, as the glacier deteriorates)
what_to_bring: Ski or snowshoe option for a spring descent

detailed_rack: Standard glacier-mountaineering kit: ice axe, crampons, a rope with crevasse-rescue gear, and a helmet; a light rock rack is optional for the final class 3-4 scrambling to the east summit.
pro_needs: Primarily snow and glacier protection; minimal rock pro for the short scramble finish.

detailed_rack: Crampons, ice tools/axes (2), ice screws (4-6, 12-16 cm), snow flukes/pickets (2-3), rock nuts (half set from 0.5-2 inches), hexes (2-3), carabiners (8-10, mix of lockers and non-lockers), 50m single or 60m double rope, webbing and slings, harness, belay devices.
pro_needs: Alpine rock protection: single set of nuts and hexes (0.5-2 inches), small rack (6-8 pieces), and 50-meter rope for belay anchors on exposed ridge sections. Crampons required for glacier and snow sections.
rack: Half set of rock nuts (0.5-2in) and 2-3 hexes
Minimal light rock rack for the summit scramble
4-6 ice screws (12-16cm) and 2-3 snow pickets/flukes for the glacier crossing
what_to_bring: Satellite communicator/InReach — no cell coverage on approach or climb
Trekking poles for the Bachelor Creek ford and off-trail heather/scree traverse
Water treatment for the multi-day approach camps

detailed_rack: #2 carabiners, #2 and small stoppers for lead protection. For top-rope setup: two 60m ropes or two shorter ropes (single rope climbing via natural anchor). Quickdraws for leading. Helmet required.
pro_needs: Light traditional pro: #2 carabiners and small stoppers are sufficient for the thin crack crux. The route does not require extensive rack; a single set of small to mid-sized cams could supplement protection on the crux if desired. Most climbers use top-rope given the short length and natural anchor at top.
rack: Cams, single small-to-mid set (optional, to supplement crux)
what_to_bring: sleeping bag (rated for potential sub-freezing nights)
fire starter or lighter (for stove use only)

detailed_rack: Glacier kit (harness, prusiks, pickets, slings) plus a few small pieces for the short Class 4 summit rock.
pro_needs: Roped glacier travel on the Neve Glacier, then a short exposed Class 4 scramble to the summit block; minimal rock pro needed.
what_to_bring: Full water carry for the dry approach

detailed_rack: Glacier kit (harness, prusiks, pickets, slings); minimal rock gear needed.
pro_needs: Standard glacier-travel kit — rope, a few pickets or ice screws, and crevasse-rescue gear; no rock protection is needed for the Class 2-3 summit scramble.
what_to_bring: Rope, harness, and crevasse-rescue kit for the Snowking Glacier
Overnight/bivy gear — most parties take two days
Water treatment (snowmelt only above Cyclone Lake)

detailed_rack: Conditions-dependent: fully snow-filled sections may need nothing beyond an axe/crampons; exposed rock or ice sections call for pickets and rock protection up to 2 inches.
pro_needs: Protection needs vary enormously by season and snow coverage — check current conditions before committing to a technical rating expectation.
what_to_bring: Avalanche awareness for the approach slopes in spring

detailed_rack: Ice axe and crampons for the snow, plus a 60m rope for handline sections and the summit rappel; a light rack of small-to-medium nuts and cams up to about a #2 Camalot covers the chockstone/crux exit, with 2-3 slings for tree or rock rappel anchors. Conditions-dependent — some parties report needing little beyond the chockstone move.
pro_needs: A small rock rack, a single rope, and slings for trees; many parties simul-climb or solo the easier gully sections rather than pitching the whole route out.

detailed_rack: 10-12 quickdraws cover the bolted sections, with a small-to-mid cam set (~0.4-2.5in) and stopper set for gaps between bolts, matching the crag's mixed sport/trad character; helmet is warranted given the loose welded tuff-breccia typical of this crag.
what_to_bring: Approach shoes for the road walk-in

detailed_rack: A medium rock rack up to 4 inches with many extra runners for a wandering line; an ice axe if climbing early season.
pro_needs: Standard rack to 4" with plentiful slings/runners; natural pro (trees) supplements gear in the brushy sections.
what_to_bring: Bivy gear (route can extend into the night)
Approach shoes for the brushy approach to the face

detailed_rack: No technical rack; ice axe useful early season for snow in the basin.
pro_needs: None.
what_to_bring: Helmet for the Headlee Pass chute and upper scramble
Ice axe/crampons if any snow remains on the approach
Extra socks or camp shoes for the stream ford
Sun/bug protection for the lower valley in midsummer

detailed_rack: Ice axe and crampons standard; a second tool is prudent if the face is icy rather than soft snow. Glacier/crevasse-rescue gear for the approach across the Middle Cascade Glacier and the bergschrund crossing.
what_to_bring: Overnight camp gear (Kool-Aid Lake/Cache Col base camp)

detailed_rack: A glacier travel kit (rope, harness, crevasse-rescue gear) for the Middle Cascade Glacier crossing; ice axe and crampons for the Cache Col snowfields and any residual snow in the gully; helmet is essential given constant rockfall. Once off the glacier the gully/ridge is climbed unroped as a scramble by most parties — a light rock rack is optional, not standard.
pro_needs: This is primarily an unroped glacier-approach scramble rather than a pitched rock climb; the real protection needs are a helmet against rockfall and standard crevasse-rescue gear for the glacier, not a traditional rack.
what_to_bring: Overnight/bivy gear for a base camp at Kool-Aid Lake or Spider-Formidable Col
Extra food for a 2-3 day itinerary

detailed_rack: A rope for exposed, rope-assisted sections and a light rack of nuts/cams and slings for improvised anchors on class 3-4 terrain; helmet given the loose rock typical of this peak.

Not a roped rock climb for most parties, but the exposed, loose Class 3-4 moves near the south-ridge notch and the crux ramp are commonly protected with a light rack and a short rope for less-experienced scramblers; many parties climb it entirely unroped with a helmet.
pro_needs: A 30m rope with a small rack of slings/light gear is enough to belay the short crux sections; an ice axe (and traction in early season) is needed for the approach snowfields.
rack: Optional light rack (slings) + 30m rope for the crux ramp/notch (used by less-experienced parties)

detailed_rack: No technical rack required — the standard route is a scramble. Bring an ice axe (and crampons if the NE couloir hasn't melted out); no rope or glacier gear is needed on the Royal Basin approach.
pro_needs: None for the standard route; a rope and small rack would only come into play on the distinctly harder, separately-named 5.x South Side Face.
what_to_bring: Ice axe (and crampons if attempting before mid-July or after fresh snow)
Bear canister for Royal Basin camping
Sturdy boots for talus and scree
Trekking poles for unbridged creek crossings

detailed_rack: A minimal rack of nuts with long slings for the rock buttress, plus crampons, ice screws, pickets, ice axe and a second tool for the lower icefall/ice sections.
pro_needs: Sparse protection on both the ice and the easy 5th-class buttress; runouts are expected.
what_to_bring: glacier travel gear for the Lower Curtis approach
headlamp/nav aids for the descent Hourglass

detailed_rack: A light glacier/scramble rack is typical rather than a full rock rack: a 30-50m rope for the glacier crossing and any short technical sections, a small rack of cams and nuts for protecting occasional low 5th-class moves on the traverse's harder sections, plus standard glacier travel gear (harness, crevasse-rescue kit, pickets) for the snowfield crossing to the West Fury col.
pro_needs: Minimal fixed protection needed on Swiss itself given its comparatively solid, moderate-angle rock; gear is carried primarily for the connecting glacier crossings and any exposed 4th/low-5th sections elsewhere on the traverse rather than for Swiss's summit block specifically.
what_to_bring: bear canister (required for overnight backcountry camping in North Cascades NP)

detailed_rack: No roped rock climbing is normally required. Parties typically carry a light steep-snow kit — an ice axe and crampons — for the north-slope couloir and any lingering snow patches, plus a helmet for the loose, dirt-covered rock low on the route. Some parties carry a rope and a few slings/small rock pieces for extra confidence on the ridge scramble/old cornice remnant, though the standard line is not roped.
pro_needs: No fixed protection on the standard dry scramble; parties climbing earlier in the season when snow/cornices linger near the summit have carried a rope, a picket, and slings for running belays on the exposed headwall.
what_to_bring: Ice axe and crampons (spring/early summer conditions)
Helmet for loose rock on the gendarmes
Light rope (~30m) and a few slings for the occasional short rappel past the crux band
Gaiters/brush-tolerant clothing for the bushwhack along Tailgunner Creek

detailed_rack: Snow gear early season (axe, crampons); no rock rack needed for the standard scramble
pro_needs: None typical for the standard line; a rope is optional for less experienced parties on the upper steps
what_to_bring: Helmet (strongly recommended — recurring rockfall reports in the couloir and Hourglass)
Ice axe and crampons (roughly April-June while the couloir/Hourglass still hold snow)
30m rope or handline (optional, for less-experienced climbers through the Hourglass)
Sturdy boots suited to class 3-4 scrambling on loose rock

detailed_rack: A standard alpine trad rack (small-to-medium nuts and cams) covers the short technical pitch at The Horn's notch; long slings help manage rope drag on the wandering line. Crampons and an ice axe are recommended for the snow slope below Sawtooth Pass outside of late summer.
pro_needs: Rack to 3in; both the SE and SW routes are R-rated (runout/sparsely protected), so plan on a mix of small-to-medium cams/nuts plus a few pitons and tat for anchors — this is not a well-protected or bolted route.
rack: Small-to-medium rack, doubles in finger-to-hand sizes (to 3")
A few small pitons and tat for aging anchors
Two ropes for a double-rope rappel off the summit notch
what_to_bring: rope and trad rack for the 5.5 summit pitch

detailed_rack: No technical rock climbing gear required; this is a scramble. Bring a helmet and grippy footwear (rock shoes or sticky approach shoes). Trekking poles helpful for scree. Microspikes or crampons if snow present. No protection rack needed; carry a single 30-40m rope and a few slings for the short roped section on Peak 1.
pro_needs: This is a scramble, not a technical rock route — no traditional rack needed. Bring a single 30-40m rope and a few slings/rap rings for the short roped section most parties end up using on Peak 1 (the hardest, westernmost peak); the other peaks are typically climbed unroped by confident, rope-experienced scramblers in dry conditions.
what_to_bring: Northwest Forest Pass for trailhead parking
Extra water — none reliably available above Twin Lakes/High Pass in late summer
Layers — exposed, windy ridge near the Canadian border

detailed_rack: A light rock rack (small-to-medium cams and a handful of nuts) covers the few low fifth-class moves; the bulk of the gear need is for the Terror Glacier crossing and Barrier traverse — rope, harness, crevasse-rescue kit, ice axe, and crampons.
pro_needs: A light alpine rock rack is sufficient for the standard Class 3/4 terrain; if attempting the harder East Ridge/Face (~5.8), bring a few small cams and nuts.
what_to_bring: NPS-approved bear canister (required in some zones; loaner canisters only available with in-person pickup in Marblemount)
Satellite communicator (inReach/SPOT) -- no cell coverage in the Southern Pickets
Map/compass or GPS -- the approach trail is easy to lose in poor visibility

detailed_rack: Alpine climbing rack suitable for Grade IV rock: selection of carabiners and quickdraws, 60m multi-pitch rope setup, pitons for protection on vertical sections and loose terrain, helmet for rockfall hazard in gully approach
pro_needs: Grade IV rock climbing ability required. Protection essential on vertical to overhanging sections. Firm grounding in alpine rock climbing, loose terrain assessment, and objective hazard evaluation necessary.
rack: Ice axe for the snow/scree approach

detailed_rack: No full rack is required for the scramble. A short rope and a few slings are useful to protect or hand-line the exposed steps, and an ice axe is worth carrying early in the season for snow.
pro_needs: The standard line is largely unprotected scrambling, with the option to sling horns or place the occasional small piece on the most exposed steps. Comfort on exposed fourth-class terrain is the key requirement rather than a large rack.

detailed_rack: Single rack of nuts (~10 pieces) and cams from about 0.3 to 3 in (BD sizing), 6-8 shoulder-length (60cm) slings, 4-5 double-length (120cm) slings, single 60m rope. A pared-down rack of cams 0.5-2 in plus a nut set is workable for confident leaders. Add an ice axe and light crampons for early-season snow on the approach and at the Pineapple Pass notch.
pro_needs: Protection is straightforward low-5th-class trad gear — small-to-medium cams and nuts protect the cracks, flakes, and grooves; the ledgy nature of the climbing keeps runouts short, though the rock is not fully solid everywhere, so test placements and be cautious with loose blocks.

detailed_rack: A light rack of cams to 2 inches, a set of nuts, several slings for the towers, and a 60m rope for the short step and rappel. Add ice axe and crampons for the approach.
pro_needs: Protection on the short technical step is adequate in cracks and around horns, while the scrambling sections are largely unprotected. Comfort on exposed terrain matters more than a large rack.

detailed_rack: A rack suited to 5.6 R climbing (small-to-medium cams and nuts) plus a rope for the crux pitch and any short lowers on the loose descent toward the Eldorado Glacier; a helmet is essential given documented rockfall and loose blocks along the ridge.
pro_needs: The 5.6 R crux and much of the ridge offer limited or run-out protection — treat gear as supplemental to careful, deliberate movement rather than a guarantee.
what_to_bring: Helmet (mandatory — documented rockfall and loose blocks)
Extra water and bivy gear if linking with Eldorado or a multi-day traverse
Sturdy approach shoes plus rock shoes or a stiff boot for the crux pitch

detailed_rack: No technical rack; ice axe useful early season for snow in the approach basins.
pro_needs: None.
what_to_bring: Helmet (loose rock is the dominant hazard on every line)
Trekking poles for the river fords
Ice axe if snow remains on the southeast-approach snow ramp (common into July)
Light rope and a few pieces of gear if planning the South Chimney (Class 4) variant, plus rap rings/webbing for the two ~60 ft rappels

detailed_rack: No fixed rock protection is typically placed; parties carry an ice axe and crampons (or ski/ascent plates) for the couloir, with a rope and pickets optional depending on conditions.
pro_needs: Primarily a snow/ice couloir climb - protection is via ice axe/crampon technique rather than a placed rack; carry a rope and a few pickets if icy or firm conditions warrant belays.
what_to_bring: Extra layers for a long, early-alpine-start day
Map/GPS for off-trail navigation via Cascade Pass/Alliteration Col to Trapper Lake

detailed_rack: Single alpine rock rack with medium focus; 10-12 slings and rappel cord; one to two ropes depending on party size; ice axes; crampons; helmet.
pro_needs: Protection is sparse and frequently improvised — slung horns, trees, and chockstones on the loose ridge crest — a standard single alpine rack is sufficient for the harder moves.
rack: 10-12 slings/rappel tat for varying anchor quality
Ice axe and crampons for approach/descent
what_to_bring: bivy sack and emergency sleep system
water bottles and iodine tabs or water filter
warm layers and emergency down jacket
first aid kit with blister treatment

detailed_rack: No rope or rack is needed for the standard summer ascent — this is unroped Class 2-3 scrambling over boulders, a rock ledge, and steep dirt. In residual snow (spring) or winter conditions, carry an ice axe and traction (microspikes or crampons) for the steep upper slopes.
what_to_bring: Ice axe and crampons for spring/early-summer ascents (snow in the summit gully persists into summer)
Map/GPS and route-finding experience — no maintained tread or consistent cairns
Sturdy boots for cliff-band and talus travel
Plan for a full, long day (10-12+ hours car-to-car)

detailed_rack: A standard light alpine rack: a handful of cams and nuts to around 2 inches, slings for the ledge traverses, harness, and a 30 m rope has proven sufficient for the technical sections.
pro_needs: Protection is sparse at the crux flake/crack — described as 'dubiously protected' — so don't expect bomber gear exactly where it's needed most.
what_to_bring: sturdy approach shoes for brush and talus
ice axe/crampons if snow lingers on the approach traverse

detailed_rack: Doubles of cams to #2, single #3 and #4 cams, and a nut set. Helmet essential given loose blocks near the P1 start.
pro_needs: Sparse in spots, notably thin gear on the P4 corner-to-roof crux; a fuller rack (doubles to #2, singles #3/#4) covers the rest.
what_to_bring: water treatment for the Early Winters Creek crossing
light rock shoes for the delicate face pitch (P3)

detailed_rack: Single rack to #1 with a few duplicates in the finger sizes. Recommended: 2–3 nuts in fingers, 2–3 mid-hand nuts, 2–3 hand-sized cams, 1–2 #1 cams. Approach climbing may require ice axe (early season). Small to medium nuts and slings optional but not required. 15 draws (mix of singles and doubles) recommended; 6 of these can be single runners.
pro_needs: Primarily bolted sport climbing with some trad pitches. Anchors are bolted throughout; the bolts were replaced with stainless steel and upgraded during 2020 modernization. Climbers must be comfortable with self-rescue, anchor building, and transitioning between bolted and trad protection. The route involves high commitment and serious altitude—turnaround decisions should be made early.
what_to_bring: Approach shoes for the wet gully/creek approach
Water or hydration system (2–3L for dry/late-season)
High-calorie food (energy bars, nuts, nut butter)
First aid kit (blood stoppers, pain relief, blister treatment)
Map and compass (GPS unreliable in dense forest)
Insulation bivy layer (in case of unplanned bivy; caves reported near route start)

detailed_rack: A short rope and a light alpine rack (a few nuts and small cams, slings) are commonly carried to protect or belay the exposed summit-block moves; bring an ice axe for early-season approach snow.
pro_needs: Protection for short low-5th-class steps on the summit block; most of the route is Class 3-4 scrambling.
what_to_bring: Overnight camping gear if doing it as a 2-day trip from Home Lake (tent, stove, bear canister)
Extra layers — exposed subalpine camp and summit day with real weather exposure
Map/compass/altimeter (NPS specifically recommends 7.5' quads over 15' maps for this area)

detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard summer route. Carry an ice axe for the summit gully/chute whenever snow is present (common into July), with crampons or microspikes if the snow is firm; a helmet is recommended given the loose rock in the gully.
pro_needs: None - the standard route is unroped scrambling; no fixed or removable protection is placed.
what_to_bring: sturdy mountaineering or approach boots for scree/talus
bug spray (Copper Glance basin mosquitoes reported)
extra water — limited shade/water sources on the upper mountain
layers for a wind-exposed summit ridge

detailed_rack: A light alpine rock rack (small-to-mid cams and nuts) covers the low-5th-class pitches and 5.7 crux; carry a few extra slings/quickdraws for the chockstone-choked gully sections and an ice axe, plus crampons if snow lingers, for snow in the Crescent Creek Basin approach gullies depending on season.
pro_needs: Standard rock rack to ~2-3 inches is sufficient for the technical pitching; two 60m ropes are commonly carried both to link pitches efficiently and to make the col rappels on descent.

detailed_rack: No roped protection is used on the standard scramble route; parties typically carry trekking poles for the meadow/traverse sections, a helmet for the loose ridge and gully terrain, and an ice axe (with willingness to turn back if conditions warrant crampons) when snow lingers in the gullies in early season.
pro_needs: None — this is an unroped Class 3 scramble with no fixed protection or technical rack; a rope and basic protection could be carried by conservative parties for the class 4 variations, but are not standard.
what_to_bring: Ice axe and traction (crampons/microspikes) for snow-covered gullies in spring/early summer
Layers for an exposed, wind-prone ridge

detailed_rack: Parties have climbed the route with a single 30m rope, one snow picket, and about six assorted slings for protecting the snowfinger crux and building rappel anchors off the summit and upper snow face; crampons and an ice axe are standard for the couloir and ridge snow.
pro_needs: A light rack — a picket or two for the snowfinger crux and slings for rappel anchors (no fixed anchors reported) — plus crampons and an ice axe for the snow sections.
what_to_bring: Bushwhacking layers for brush on the lower approach
Overnight camping gear if combining with Gunn/Tailgunner Peaks
Northwest Forest Pass for trailhead parking

detailed_rack: A medium winter alpine rock rack to 3 inches with doubles in the small cam sizes, extra runners/slings, a helmet, and two ice tools for the mixed and ice sections; 60m rope for the South Face rappel descent.
pro_needs: Protection is limited on the ~30 ft traverse into the crux corner and thin through the mixed crux itself; carry doubles in small cams plus extra slings to extend runners over featured but sparsely protectable rock.
what_to_bring: approach skis or snowshoes for the Source Lake basin approach
map/GPS for basin navigation in poor visibility

detailed_rack: Snow pickets, ice screws, and snargs; two ice tools; a few thin pitons can be useful at the rock-band crux.
pro_needs: Running belays with pickets, snargs, or screws through the 40-45 degree neve sections; a rope is prudent for parties not comfortable soloing AI2 snow/ice.
what_to_bring: crevasse rescue kit for the glacier-adjacent approach

pro_needs: Unroped scramble; no fixed protection used. An ice axe (and sometimes crampons) is advisable for the snow couloir/gully section into summer.
what_to_bring: Topo map/GPS track — route-finding is the main difficulty
Extra water — long, exposed slog with little shade up high
Bug protection for the brushy lower approach

pro_needs: None required -- this is a Class 2-3 scramble with no fixed protection; a helmet is recommended given the loose rock and the chance of other parties above on the boot path.
what_to_bring: Northwest Forest Pass (day or annual) displayed in the vehicle at the trailhead
Green Trails Map No. 168S (The Brothers) or a Buckhorn Wilderness map
Ice axe/microspikes if snow lingers (common into early-mid July)
Sun protection and warm layers — exposed, often windy ridge

pro_needs: Class 3 talus/ridge scramble, with one short Class 4 step on Point 8207 that can be skirted on its north side; a helmet is recommended for the loose-rock ridge traverse between Lago and Dot. No rope or technical protection normally needed.

Most parties scramble this unroped and there is no fixed protection, but the Class 4 moves at the summit have been protected with a short rope, a few slings and a couple of small cams. A helmet is strongly advised for rockfall on the loose talus and in the gully/col below the summit block.
what_to_bring: map/compass or GPS track — no trail or signage on route
extra water — little reliable water source after early-season snowmelt, and post-fire slopes offer less shade
bug/insect protection for brushy sections in July

pro_needs: Not a roped rock route; parties carry glacier-travel gear (rope, harness, basic crevasse-rescue kit) for the Hagan Glacier crossing rather than rock protection.
rack: Glacier travel gear (rope, harness, crevasse rescue kit)
Small rock climbing rack for final Class 3 summit slabs

pro_needs: No technical protection is needed — this is an unroped class 3 scramble on talus and blocky rock; a helmet is a reasonable precaution against rockfall on the ridge.
what_to_bring: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass for trailhead parking
Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit (available at the trailhead)
Topo map/GPS track — cairns thin out through the boulder fields
Ice axe if traveling before mid-to-late July

pro_needs: No technical pro; an ice axe helps with any lingering snow near the pass early season.
No technical rock pro on the standard line; an ice axe helps on early-season snow slopes.
what_to_bring: Bear canister (required for overnight camping in the Duckabush/Marmot Lake corridor)
Topo map and compass or GPS — no trail beyond O'Neil Pass
Insect repellent for the Marmot Lake basin
Water treatment (reliable water along the river/lakes, but treat before drinking)

pro_needs: No technical protection needed; early season an ice axe and the skill to self-arrest are strongly recommended for the snow chute.
No technical protection is used on the standard Class 2 route; some parties carry an ice axe for lingering early-season snow near the ridge shared with White Mountain.
what_to_bring: Map and compass or GPS (off-trail travel above the pass)
Bear canister (required for all overnight stays)
Extra water capacity — none available at La Crosse Pass
Ice axe/microspikes if climbing before mid-July
Satellite messenger given the lack of cell coverage

pro_needs: No fixed protection or roped climbing is documented on this route; it is typically done as an unroped scramble, though a helmet is recommended given the loose rock (choss) in the summit gully and boulder field.
No technical protection is required on this Class 2 scramble; an ice axe is worthwhile in early season for lingering snow on the upper slopes.
None — this is an unroped scramble route; no technical rack is used, though an ice axe is carried for early-season snow.
what_to_bring: Map/compass or GPS track (the route beyond Pinnacle Lake is unmarked and off-trail)
Bug spray for the Bathtub Lakes basin

pro_needs: No technical rock pro on the standard line; an ice axe helps on early-season snow slopes.
what_to_bring: Ice axe (crampons too if climbing before mid-July)
Bear canister — required for overnight food storage in this wilderness
Water treatment (giardia risk in all streams)
Map/compass or GPS for the unmarked amphitheater and ridge sections
Satellite communicator — cell coverage is essentially nonexistent in this basin

pro_needs: The summer NW Ridge route needs no rock protection — it's an unroped scramble over talus, dirt, and one short exposed ridge crest. In winter and spring, carry an ice axe and crampons; some parties rope up or fix a hand line on the snow gully below the summit ridge.
rack: Short rope/handline for the loose 4th-class crux gully and its informal rappel stations
what_to_bring: Ice axe and crampons for winter/spring ascents when the gully is snow or ice-filled
A 30 m rope and basic rappel gear — useful even in summer for the crux gully, where informal rappel anchors exist near the top
Sturdy boots and gaiters for brush and mud on the lower approach
A GPS track from a recent trip report rather than relying solely on the mapped road line near Olney Creek
Bug spray — brushy, buggy approach in summer

pro_needs: None required under normal summer conditions on the standard south ridge line — it's an unroped Class 2 scramble; carrying an ice axe for lingering snow patches is prudent.
what_to_bring: Ice axe (lingering snow on upper slopes, especially before August)
Sturdy boots suited to cross-country talus, heather, and brush
Wilderness permit and a hard-sided bear canister (required at every wilderness camp in the park)
Map/compass or GPS — no cell signal and no maintained tread once off the Elwha River Trail

pro_needs: No fixed protection is placed; this is an unroped scramble for competent parties. An ice axe (and in early season, possibly crampons) is commonly carried for the approach snow slopes.
No technical protection is used - this is an unroped scramble. An ice axe is essential whenever snow/neve is present in the couloir; some parties also carry a helmet for the loose talus sections.
None in dry summer conditions; carry an ice axe (and possibly crampons) if snow lingers on the upper slopes.
Non-technical class 2 scramble/snow climb — no rock rack is used. In firm, icy, or wind-scoured conditions on the Skyline Ridge slopes, some parties add lightweight crampons alongside an ice axe.
what_to_bring: Sturdy boots or approach shoes for loose talus and scree
Trekking poles for the steep, loose lower trail
Layers — the exposed summit ridge catches wind even on warm days
All the water you'll need — none is reliable above the trailhead
Sun protection for the open upper slopes

pro_needs: No technical rack or rope needed on the standard Class 2-3 route; a helmet is recommended for the loose summit block, but no roped climbing is required.

detailed_rack: A small set of stoppers and a handful of slings in several lengths protects the wet fourth-class pitches and builds rappel anchors; add cord and rap rings to leave behind.
pro_needs: Stoppers and slings are enough for the fourth-class pitches; a single 60 m rope covers the climbing and the rappels on the way down.
rack: Cord and rap rings for rappel anchors
Glacier kit (axe, crampons) for the approach

detailed_rack: Light-to-moderate alpine trad rack: stoppers/nuts, cams up to ~3 inches, plenty of slings, and spare webbing/cord for weathered rappel anchors.
pro_needs: A moderate trad rack (stoppers plus cams roughly 0.5–1 inch) covers the crux chimney and ledge systems; bring extra slings for tat at rappel anchors.

detailed_rack: A single rack from 0.3 to 3 inches, doubles in the 1-2 inch range (larger hand/fist-sized cams especially useful for the crux crack), six or so smaller stoppers, a mix of alpine draws and double-length runners, plus extra cord/tat for rappel anchors on the West Ridge descent.
pro_needs: Standard alpine trad rack weighted toward hand-to-fist-sized cams for the crux pitch, plus glacier travel gear (crampons, ice axe, rope, crevasse-rescue kit) for the Terror Glacier crossing.
rack: Single cam rack .2/.3–3in, doubled in 1-2in and 2-3in
what_to_bring: Sun protection for exposed glacier crossing

detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for this scramble/glacier route. Parties rope up for the Borealis Glacier crossing near Lucky Pass and carry standard glacier travel gear (rope, pickets, prusiks) — one trip report used two 30m ropes for a party of five.
pro_needs: No fixed protection is placed; glacier travel gear (rope, pickets/ice screws as needed) covers the crevasse hazard on the Borealis Glacier traverse.
rack: A few optional pieces for the Class 3 rock finish (not essential)
what_to_bring: Satellite communicator (inReach/SPOT) — cell service is unreliable to nonexistent
Extra food/fuel buffer in case weather forces a layover

detailed_rack: A single rack of cams 0.3-3in with doubles in the 0.5-2in finger/hand range covers the sustained splitter cracks on P1/P4, plus a full nut set; carry an aider or daisy for the short ~15ft 5.11+/5.12- C1 aid crux on pitch 3 (or be ready to French-free it).
rack: Aiders/daisy for the short C1 aid section (or French-free)
what_to_bring: aiders/etriers for the short C1 section
overnight Core Zone permit if camping

detailed_rack: Only a light rock rack is needed for the class 4/low-5th climbing itself (small-to-medium cams, a few nuts, and slings for natural anchors); the more consequential kit is full glacier-travel gear for the Whatcom and Challenger Glacier crossings on approach.
pro_needs: Minimal protection is needed on the peak's easy fifth-class terrain; prioritize glacier rescue gear (rope, prusiks/mechanical ascenders, pickets) over a large rock rack.
rack: Light rack of small-to-medium cams and a few nuts
Single dynamic rope for class 4 climbing/rappels
Glacier travel gear (ice axe, crampons) for Whatcom/Challenger Glacier crossings

detailed_rack: Mostly bolt-protected with small camming units and a few stoppers for gaps; bring about 14 draws and some long slings, primarily needed on P1.
pro_needs: Very solid, well-bolted protection overall, though some moves must be committed above the last piece.
rack: Single rope (60m); two ropes for rappel from the route (per route beta)
what_to_bring: two ropes for the rappel descent

detailed_rack: Standard trad rack to 5 inches; a single Black Diamond #4 cam is useful near the top and could allow running out the final easier ground.
pro_needs: Gear to 5 inches; solid finger-to-hand-size placements protect the lieback-flake crux and the roof traverse best.
rack: Optional BD #4 for the upper slab
what_to_bring: A stiff brush for lingering moss on holds
Helmet — Monte Cristo-area rock is generally chossy

detailed_rack: Snow anchors (pickets); occasional ice screw for firmer or icy sections.
pro_needs: Ice screws and pickets for the steep headwall

detailed_rack: A handful of pickets for the moderate/steep snow, plus 2-3 ice screws to protect the 45-65° crux chute when it is icy rather than snow-filled.
pro_needs: Glacier kit and pickets for steeper sections

detailed_rack: Small, selective rock rack: 2–3 nuts (sizes #4–#6 Black Diamond or equivalent), 2–3 cams (sizes #0–#2 for the Class 5.0 crack step). Rock quality is variable (mix of good granodiorite and loose choss); expect poor protection and friable anchors. Primarily a protection rack for the single short technical step; most route management via scrambling and glacier travel.
pro_needs: Minimal rock climbing protection needed. The Class 5.0 rock step can be approached unroped by experienced alpinists. One 25-meter rope can be established for the short rappel descent. Glacier travel relies on snow anchor technology (flukes) rather than rock protection. Confidence on exposed Class 3–4 scrambling and efficient rope management required; this is an expedition-style climb.
rack: 25m rope for the short rappel descent (or full glacier rope)

detailed_rack: Technical alpine rack: two tools, ice screws, pickets, a light rock rack for mixed steps, a single rope, full crevasse-rescue kit.
pro_needs: Ice screws, pickets, and a light rock rack for mixed sections
rack: Two ice tools, ice screws, pickets

detailed_rack: Technical alpine rack: two tools, a set of ice screws, pickets, a light rock rack for the mixed sections, a single rope for belays/simul, full crevasse-rescue kit.
pro_needs: Ice screws, pickets; full steep-ice alpine kit
rack: Two ice tools, ice screws, pickets

detailed_rack: Technical ice/glacier kit: two tools, a rack of ice screws, pickets, full crevasse-rescue gear for the heavily broken glacier.
pro_needs: Ice screws and pickets; efficient serac/crevasse navigation
rack: A few pitons (belay anchors in serac terrain)

detailed_rack: Light alpine technical rack: two tools, several ice screws, pickets, a small rock rack (two pitons, half a set of nuts, a few small cams) for the short rock pitch above 12,000 ft, a single rope for running belays, full crevasse-rescue kit.
pro_needs: Ice screws and pickets for steep ice/snow; full alpine ice kit
rack: Two ice tools, ice screws, pickets

detailed_rack: Glacier kit with pickets for steep snow; several ice screws for the upper Mowich Face; full crevasse-rescue gear for the long glaciated approach.
pro_needs: Ice screws and pickets; full alpine ice kit for the headwall
rack: 3 x 120cm slings (anchor extension on the upper Mowich Face finish)
Two ice tools, ice screws, pickets

detailed_rack: Glacier kit with pickets and a couple of screws for steeper icefall sections; full crevasse-rescue gear for the complex glacier.
pro_needs: Full glacier kit; pickets and possibly a second tool for the steep sickle

detailed_rack: Light, fast technical kit: two tools, ice screws, pickets, a single rope for simul/belays, full crevasse-rescue gear; speed is the main 'protection'.
pro_needs: Full steep alpine ice kit; speed is the primary safety tool

detailed_rack: No rock rack needed for the standard line; carry crevasse-rescue and glacier travel gear.
pro_needs: Glacier travel protection (pickets, screws in late-season ice) rather than rock gear.
rack: Single 30m glacier rope (or 60m combined with Fisher Chimneys exit)
what_to_bring: extra layers for the exposed traverse near Hell's Highway

detailed_rack: A light alpine rock rack (a handful of cams and stoppers) suffices for the low-5th-class ridge; glacier travel gear is needed for the approach to Crescent Creek Basin.
pro_needs: Protection needs are modest given the grade — small-to-mid cams and stoppers protect the steep summit ridge; the slabs below are mostly unprotected low-angle scrambling.
rack: Light alpine rack: a few cams and stoppers
Glacier travel gear for the Crescent Creek Basin approach

detailed_rack: Standard trad rack to 3 inches, emphasizing small-to-medium cams and stoppers for the finger and thin-hand crack/seam systems on pitches 3, 4, and 6; a few pitons can back up older or marginal placements. Doubling the smaller sizes is worthwhile given the sustained 5.10 corner and seam pitches.
pro_needs: Mostly small gear (finger to hand size); the route protects well on natural gear in its crack/corner systems, with a couple of fixed pieces reported on the 5.10+ third pitch.
rack: Trad rack to 3in, doubled in finger-to-hand sizes
A few pitons for old fixed placements/thin seams
Ice axe, crampons for the glacier approach/descent
60m double ropes (walk-off descent; the pair allows a rappel retreat)
what_to_bring: Glacier travel gear (axe, crampons, rope for the approach glacier)
Full alpine rock rack plus a few pitons
Multi-day bivy/camping gear for the approach
Water-taxi reservation or a carried-in boat for the Ross Lake crossing

detailed_rack: A light rack for the West Peak summit block: a few nuts or three or four small-to-medium cams, plus 3-4 slings for anchors. Most of the scrambling between summits is done unroped.
pro_needs: Self-reliance and route-finding ability are critical. Parties should be proficient in crevasse rescue and comfortable with unroped scrambling on exposed terrain.
rack: Glacier travel kit: rope, crevasse-rescue gear
what_to_bring: Standard glacier climb gear (ice axe, crampons, rope, harness, crevasse rescue kit)
Light rock rack for the West Peak summit block (most scrambling between summits does not require roped belays)
Extra water (3L minimum) due to long summit day
High-calorie food for 16+ hours of climbing

detailed_rack: Double rack of small to medium cams plus nuts; extra small pieces for the thin crux cracks.
pro_needs: Emphasis on small-to-medium protection for the sustained hard crack pitches.
rack: Double rack of small-to-medium cams (RP set + standard nuts)
Extra small pieces for thin crux cracks
1 cordelette for backing up mixed bolt/gear rap anchors

detailed_rack: Standard glacier-travel kit plus a minimal alpine rack: one to two snow pickets per rope team for crevasse-rescue anchors, a few slings and locking carabiners, and (optionally) a thin rack of small-to-mid cams/nuts for the short rock step in Icy Peak's summit gully. Most competent parties move together on the glacier and solo or simul-climb the 3rd-4th class terrain in good conditions.
pro_needs: Protection needs are minimal and glacier-oriented — pickets for crevasse rescue and occasional running pro — rather than a technical rock rack; the summit gully on Icy is typically soloed or simul-climbed rather than pitched out.
rack: 2-3 snow pickets and crevasse-rescue kit for the Ruth Glacier crossing
Harness plus slings/rap rings or tat for an optional rappel of Icy's summit gully (~100ft)
what_to_bring: Bivy/camping gear for the overnight high camp
Wag bags (alpine zone has no toilets)
Extra layers for exposed, windy camps

detailed_rack: No traditional rock rack is needed. A single 150 ft rope is what covers leading and then rappelling the one short (~50-60 ft) class 4 section - doubled through the tree anchor a 100 ft rope reaches only about 50 ft; that pitch can be protected with about three slings over horns or trees rather than cams or nuts.
pro_needs: Minimal gear beyond a rope and a few slings for the short class 4 step; no cams or nuts are required.
rack: 30m rope (100-150ft sufficient) for the short roped pitch/rappel
1-2 long slings/webbing for tree rap anchor (bring your own, don't reuse old tat)
what_to_bring: Map/compass or GPS track — this is off-trail, unmarked cross-country travel from Gothic Basin onward
Headlamp — many parties finish in the dark given 10-17 hour days
Extra water — no reliable water source is documented on the ridge traverse
Bivy/overnight gear if splitting the trip with a camp in Gothic Basin
A pencil for the summit register (past visitors note it's often left without one)

detailed_rack: Alpine rack with emphasis on small and medium cams, stoppers, and slings. Good anchoring equipment for rappels.
pro_needs: This route has solid granite and good protection opportunities throughout. The cannon hole pitch may require placement at a specific angle to span the gap.
rack: Glacier travel gear (axe, crampons) for approach
what_to_bring: Water and food for multi-day approach

detailed_rack: A light trad rack suffices: double-length slings for the ridge, small-to-medium nuts and cams to about 1.5 inches (tricams work well), plus full glacier travel and crevasse-rescue gear for the approach.
pro_needs: Protection is mostly for the last three low-5th-class pitches; gear to 1.5 inches with extra slings covers it.
rack: Glacier travel + crevasse rescue kit for approach
what_to_bring: approach shoes/boots for the Shannon Ridge trail
sun protection for glare off the glaciers

detailed_rack: A long route (14 pitches of full 60m/200ft length on the 2012 ascent; the 1975 FA logged 22 pitches)
pro_needs: Protection is generally good with cams and nuts on the more solid sections; be selective and test placements on the loose red rock bands noted by repeat ascent parties.
rack: Cams, doubles finger-to-hand sizes (small Aliens most useful), plus #3/#4
what_to_bring: approach shoes for the Hart Lake-to-buttress approach
bivy gear for Hart Lake camp
light rack of slings for horn/block anchors

detailed_rack: A light rack — slings and a small selection of cams/nuts — is enough for protecting the short 5th-class chimney move; the rest of the route is unroped scrambling.
pro_needs: Minimal gear placements needed, concentrated at the one 5th-class chimney move; considerable exposure on this section warrants a rope even though the technical difficulty is modest.
rack: Small rack: slings, small cams/nuts for the chimney
Ice axe and crampons for the glacier approach
